A written assessment, including direct observation, of whether a staff member performs required tasks correctly and safely.

procedures: Before a person starts work, the administrator verifies the age requirement: on-site managers and responsible staff are 21 or older, and anyone under 18 is assigned only to line-of-sight supervision by a named qualified staff member.

On or before the first day, the administrator or designee gives a general orientation covering resident rights (PCH-05), abuse reporting (PCH-08), emergency and fire procedures (PCH-10), infection control (PCH-07), confidentiality (RR-05), house rules (PCH-04) and the home's policies. The new hire signs an orientation acknowledgment.

The administrator builds an individual Training Plan for each new hire listing every required topic, including emergency first aid and CPR, and the date by which it will be done. All required work-related training is completed within the first 60 days of employment.

The administrator schedules emergency first aid and CPR certification through a recognized provider, with a hands-on skills demonstration, and ensures that it is completed no later than day 60. Until then, the new hire is not counted as the only trained person on a shift.

Direct care staff are trained and checked on their competency in the personal services they perform (transfers, toileting, bathing, feeding, skin care, falls prevention, incident reporting). A supervisor observes each new hire and signs a skills checklist before the hire performs a task alone.
Medication-related training and competency checks for staff who assist with medications follow PCH-06. Staff do not perform medication tasks until the checklist is signed.

If the home operates a memory care center, every staff member, including those who do not provide direct care, completes at least 4 hours of dementia-specific orientation within the first 30 days of employment.

Direct care staff in memory care complete at least 16 hours of dementia training within the first 30 days of working independently with residents with dementia, and at least 8 hours every year after. The administrator tracks each person's hours on the Dementia Training Log.
For each dementia course, the administrator keeps the course content or curriculum, the instructor's qualifications, the agenda and a signed attendance roster in the training file.

Before a proxy caregiver provides any care, the administrator verifies that the proxy has completed the training Chapter 111-8-100 requires, keeps a copy, and gives the proxy an orientation on the home's emergency, infection control, reporting and resident rights procedures (PCH-12).

Each direct care staff member completes annual in-service training on required topics, including abuse and neglect, resident rights, infection control, emergency procedures, falls, behavior management and (where applicable) dementia care. The administrator confirms the annual hours meet the current requirements of Chapter 111-8-62.

The supervisor completes a written performance and competency evaluation for each employee at 90 days and at least annually, reviews it with the employee, and both sign it. Deficiencies lead to a written improvement plan and retraining within 30 days (PCH-09).
The administrator may call for additional training at any time after an incident, complaint, survey finding or change in resident needs, and documents the topic, date and staff attending.

Training records, evaluations and certifications are kept in each employee's personnel file under STF-02, and the administrator reviews the training matrix monthly to flag anyone approaching a deadline.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures all required training and evaluations are completed on time; tracks hours; verifies proxy caregiver training; maintains records.
Observes new hires, signs skills checklists, completes performance evaluations and supervises staff under 18 in line of sight.
Deliver content, document curriculum and qualifications and maintain attendance rosters.
Attend all assigned training, hold current CPR/first aid certification and apply what they learn.

documentation: Orientation acknowledgment and individual Training Plan
CPR and emergency first aid certificates (completed within 60 days)
Skills and competency checklists
Dementia Training Log, course content, instructor qualifications, agendas and attendance rosters (memory care)
Proxy caregiver training verification (PCH-12)
Annual in-service attendance records
90-day and annual written performance evaluations
Monthly training matrix

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: House Rules and Their Enforcement
policies.applies_to: PCH
policies.purpose: To set clear, written house rules that support a safe, orderly and respectful home, to explain how they are enforced fairly, and to make sure no house rule limits the rights of residents.
policies.policy:
This policy meets PCH .07(3)(e) (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(e)) — house rules and their enforcement.

House rules are written, given to each resident and representative at admission and posted in a common area. Each resident or representative signs an acknowledgment that the rules were received and explained. The rules cover smoking, visitors, pets, alcohol and other matters of safety and courtesy. House rules may not override resident rights (PCH-05), and the home may not punish, harass or retaliate against any resident who asserts a right, files a complaint or contacts the Ombudsman.

To follow the standard in the comparable assisted living rule (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.17), the home never restricts free access to common areas and never locks a resident into or out of the resident's bedroom. Following the ALC rule's limit, no more than two residents share a bedroom, and married residents may share a room if they wish. The administrator confirms both standards against the current Chapter 111-8-62 text at each annual policy review.

Rules are enforced consistently, starting with the least restrictive response, and any enforcement must respect the resident's dignity and the discharge procedures in PCH-02.

definitions.definition: Written rules for conduct and daily life in the home that apply to residents, visitors and staff, and are consistent with resident rights.
The steps staff take to respond to a rule violation, starting with reminders and support and ending, only when necessary, with formal notice.
Any punishment, harassment or loss of services directed at a person for asserting a right or complaining.
A signed form showing that the resident or representative received and had the house rules explained.

procedures: The administrator drafts the house rules in plain language and reviews them with the governing body (GOV-02). The rules cover smoking, visitors, pets, alcohol, quiet hours, safety items such as candles and space heaters, and use of common areas. They must not conflict with PCH-05 or the DCH rules.

SMOKING: smoking is allowed only in [DESIGNATED SMOKING AREA] away from entrances and oxygen use, with supervision when the care plan requires. Smoking materials are stored as the care plan states, and no smoking is allowed inside the home (SAF-03).

VISITORS: visitors are welcome at reasonable hours, and visiting times are posted at [VISITING HOURS]. Residents may receive visitors privately in their rooms or common areas. Visiting hours do not limit a resident's access to family, an Ombudsman, a clergy member, an attorney or a physician. Visitors sign in (PCH-13).

PETS: resident-owned pets are permitted with the administrator's prior approval, current vaccination proof, and the resident's ability to care for the pet or arrange for its care, and with respect for the health needs of other residents. Service animals are always allowed.

ALCOHOL: a resident may have alcohol of his or her own if the resident's physician has not forbidden it and there is no risk with medications. Staff do not serve alcohol to a resident who is not permitted it under the care plan, and storage is arranged to keep it away from other residents.

BEDROOMS AND COMMON AREAS: staff do not lock a resident into or out of the resident's bedroom, and do not restrict free access to common areas. No more than two residents share a bedroom, and married residents may share a room. Staff knock before entering.

At admission, the administrator or on-site manager gives the resident and representative a copy of the house rules, explains them, answers questions, and has them sign the House Rules Acknowledgment. A copy goes in the resident's record and a copy to the resident.
The administrator posts the house rules in a common area and keeps a copy available for any resident or visitor who asks.

When a resident does not follow a rule, the staff member who observes it first reminds the resident privately and respectfully, tries to understand the cause (including cognitive or health issues), and reports the incident to the shift supervisor. The incident is not handled in front of other residents.

If the problem recurs, the on-site manager meets with the resident (and the representative if the resident agrees), documents the discussion and works out a solution. This may include a care plan update (ADM-02), a different activity or schedule, or a referral to the physician.

If the problem still continues or poses a safety risk, the administrator gives the resident and representative a written notice describing the rule, the incidents and the steps taken. The notice does not threaten discharge unless discharge is actually being considered under PCH-02 and ADM-03, and the resident can use the complaint process (RR-01).

No staff member may withhold services, meals, visits, mail, phone access or other rights as a penalty for a rule violation. Staff may not use restraints, isolation or confinement to enforce a rule (SAF-02). Any staff member who does so is subject to PCH-09.

The administrator may change a house rule only after consulting residents, with written notice to residents and representatives at least 14 days before it takes effect, except when an immediate safety rule is needed. Residents who object may use the complaint process, and a new acknowledgment is signed.

The administrator reviews the house rules and enforcement records at least annually and as part of the quarterly QA review (PCH-11), and updates the rules to remain consistent with Chapter 111-8-62 and resident rights.

responsibilities.duty: Approves and updates the rules; ensures acknowledgments are signed; makes sure no rule restricts rights; decides on written notices.
Explains the rules at admission, meets with residents about repeated problems and coordinates care plan changes.
Apply the rules respectfully, start with gentle reminders and report concerns.
Receive the rules, may raise concerns and may use the complaint process.

documentation: Written house rules (current version with date)
Signed House Rules Acknowledgment for each resident
Posted copy in a common area
Rule-violation incident notes and meeting records
Written notices to residents or representatives
Notice of rule changes (14 days) and new acknowledgments
Annual house rules review and QA minutes

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Protecting Resident Rights
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Home (PCH, 2–24 beds): governing body, administrator, on-site manager, all staff, volunteers and proxy caregivers
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(c) (HCBS settings, if Medicaid waiver residents are served)
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident of [AGENCY NAME] (the "Home") is told about, and able to exercise, the rights Georgia rules give residents of personal care homes. The policy also sets out how staff protect those rights day to day and how the Home responds when a right is not honored.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(f), "Protecting the rights of the residents as set forth in these rules." The governing body has adopted it under 111-8-62-.07. The Home protects the rights of every resident under Ch. 111-8-62. Where the rule text for personal care homes matches the Georgia standard used for assisted living communities (111-8-63-.25), the Home uses that standard as its operating minimum. Residents have the right to adequate and appropriate care. They may vote and choose their own activities and schedules. They may interact with the community. They have privacy in their rooms, and staff knock before entering. They have free and private communication, without staff censorship of mail, calls or visits. Married residents may share a room, and no more than two residents may share a bedroom. No resident is coerced to assign money, valuables or property to the Home. No resident is punished or harassed for enforcing rights. A right may be waived only by the resident, the resident's representative, or the legal surrogate, and only as the rules allow. A resident with no court commitment and no authorized representative may self-discharge on 30 days' written notice. No member of the governing body, administration or staff, and no family member of any of them, may serve as a resident's legal surrogate (111-8-62-.03). The assigned State Long-Term Care Ombudsman's name, address and phone number are posted in a common area. Residents may contact the Ombudsman Program (O.C.G.A. 31-8-50 et seq.) freely and privately. If Medicaid waiver residents are served, the Home also honors the HCBS settings protections of 42 CFR 441.301(c). The Home keeps each resident's signed Resident's Rights form in the resident file.

definitions.definition: The written statement of resident rights that is explained to, signed by and given to each resident or representative at admission. The signed copy is kept in the resident file.
A person appointed or authorized under law to make decisions for a resident. No governing body member, administrator, staff member or their family member may serve in this role (111-8-62-.03).
The person the resident has designated, or who is legally authorized, to act for the resident, such as a health care agent or agent under a power of attorney.
Any punishment, harassment, reduced service, threat of discharge or unfavorable treatment because a resident, family member or staff member asserted or reported a rights concern.
The assigned representative of the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, which advocates for residents of long-term care facilities.

procedures: Before or at admission, the administrator or designee reviews the Resident's Rights form with the resident and any representative, in plain language and in a language or format they understand (see RR-06). The resident or representative signs, receives a copy, and the signed original is filed in the resident file the same day.

The administrator posts the rights notice and the assigned Ombudsman's name, address and phone number in a common area that residents and visitors can see. The administrator checks the posting monthly and replaces it within 5 business days if contact information changes.

At admission, the administrator or designee asks whether the resident has a health care agent, power of attorney or other representative. A copy of any power of attorney is placed in the resident file (see RR-04). The administrator checks that no governing body member, staff member or their family member is named as legal surrogate. If one is, the administrator tells the resident or representative and does not accept that person as surrogate.

Staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's room, except in an emergency. Staff provide personal care in private. Door-knock practice is part of orientation and is checked in the routine supervisory walk-through.

Residents may send and receive mail unopened. They may use the telephone and electronic communication privately and receive visitors at reasonable times of their choosing. Staff do not read, censor or withhold communications. Any limit on visiting that a resident requests is recorded in the care plan.

Staff help residents who wish to vote, such as with registration, absentee ballots or transportation. Staff record the assistance in the activity or service notes, without recording how the resident voted.

Residents choose their own schedules, activities, bedtimes, meals within the posted menu options, and whether to take part in Home programs. Staff do not require participation. Refusals are noted in the care plan, and the administrator is told if a refusal creates a health or safety concern.

Room assignments follow the limits of two residents per bedroom. Married residents who wish to share a room are accommodated if space allows. Residents are told in advance of any room change and may object under RR-01.

No staff member may ask, pressure or allow a resident to give, sign over or loan money, property or valuables to the Home or to any staff member. The administrator reviews resident funds and property records quarterly (see RR-03). Any suspected exploitation is handled under PCH-08.

A resident who has no court commitment and no authorized representative may self-discharge by giving 30 days' written notice to the administrator. The administrator counsels the resident on safe discharge planning, helps arrange the move at the resident's request, and files the notice in the resident file. Staff do not discourage a resident from giving notice (see PCH-02).

A resident's rights may be waived only by the resident, representative or legal surrogate, and only as the rules allow. Any waiver is in writing, dated, signed and filed in the resident file. It is reviewed at each care plan review and may be withdrawn at any time. Staff never ask for a waiver as a condition of admission or continued stay.

Staff who receive a complaint about a rights violation tell the administrator or on-site manager the same day. The administrator follows the grievance steps in RR-01 and gives the resident a written response. Staff, residents and family members who report a concern in good faith are protected from retaliation. Any act of retaliation is handled under PCH-09.

If the Home serves Medicaid waiver residents, the administrator checks at admission and at each care plan review that the resident has privacy, controls their own schedule and access to visitors, and can have personal items in their room, consistent with 42 CFR 441.301(c). Any restriction is justified in the care plan and agreed to in writing.

The administrator trains all staff on resident rights during orientation and at least annually, and records attendance (see PCH-03). Volunteers and proxy caregivers receive the rights summary before any resident contact (see PCH-12).

The administrator reviews rights concerns, grievances and Ombudsman contacts each quarter as part of quality assurance (see PCH-11). The administrator records the findings and any corrective action in the central QA file.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and reviews this policy at least annually, and ensures residents' rights are protected and that no governing body member serves as a legal surrogate.
Reviews the rights form with each resident, posts Ombudsman information, investigates rights complaints, prevents retaliation, and keeps the signed forms in resident files.
Honor resident privacy, choice and free communication; report any rights concern to the administrator or on-site manager the same day.
May assert rights, file grievances, contact the Ombudsman, and give or withdraw any rights waiver in writing.

documentation: Signed Resident's Rights form in each resident file
Copies of powers of attorney, health care agent and surrogate documents in the resident file
Photograph or log of the Ombudsman posting, with monthly check dates
Written self-discharge notices and administrator's discharge planning notes
Signed, dated rights waivers, if any
Grievance and rights-concern log with outcomes
Staff rights training attendance records
Quarterly QA review notes on rights concerns

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Medication Management, Procurement and Professional Oversight
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Home (PCH, 2–24 beds): administrator, on-site manager, staff who assist with medications, consultant pharmacist and RN
policies.purpose: To keep residents' medications ordered, obtained, stored, assisted with, documented and disposed of safely, and to name the professionals who oversee those tasks at [AGENCY NAME] (the "Home").
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(g), "Medication management, procurement and the professional oversight provided for such services." The governing body has adopted it under 111-8-62-.07. A personal care home may not provide assisted living care unless it holds an ALC license (111-8-62). The Home therefore limits staff to the medication tasks Ch. 111-8-62 allows, and it adopts the Georgia assisted living standard (111-8-63-.20) as its operating minimum wherever the PCH rule mirrors it. The administrator confirms each paragraph against the current text of Ch. 111-8-62 at adoption and annually. The Home requires orders for all medications, including over-the-counter (OTC) products. Medications are stored under lock and key in their original containers. A medication administration record (MAR) is kept daily. Controlled substances are held in a locked cabinet or box of substantial construction with a daily-updated log. Medications are disposed of per FDA and EPA guidance. Residents who can self-administer do so and keep their medications securely. Staff assistance is limited to the tasks listed for unit-dose or multi-dose packaged medications, including EpiPen use under a written protocol with a 911 call. Only certified medication aides (CMAs) listed on the Georgia Certified Medication Aide Registry may administer medications, and only if the governing body has authorized it and the Home meets the oversight requirements below. [CONSULTANT PHARMACIST NAME] reviews each resident's drug regimen quarterly. [RN NAME], RN, observes staff competency.

definitions.definition: A resident takes his or her own medication without staff giving it. This includes a resident who needs only the limited assistance tasks the rules allow.
Limited tasks staff may perform for residents using unit-dose or multi-dose packaged medications, as listed in the rules. These tasks do not include administering the medication.
A person certified and listed on the Georgia Certified Medication Aide Registry. Only a CMA may administer medications where the Home authorizes it.
Medication Administration Record. It shows each medication, dose, route, time, who assisted or administered it, and refusals or omissions.
Pharmacy packaging that separates medications by dose or by a set number of doses, with the resident's name and labeling.
A pharmacist's review of a resident's complete medication list for interactions, duplications and unneeded medications.

procedures: Before admission, the administrator or designee collects a current medication list and prescriber orders for every prescription and OTC medication, including supplements and topical products. No medication is given, or assistance provided, without a written or electronically transmitted order on file in the resident file.

The administrator or designee decides at admission and at each reassessment whether the resident can safely self-administer, needs limited assistance, or needs a service the Home cannot provide. The decision and its basis are recorded in the care plan (see ADM-02). A resident who needs more than the permitted assistance is referred under PCH-02 and ADM-01.

For residents who self-administer, staff offer a lockable space in the room or a locked Home storage alternative. The resident keeps the key. A duplicate key is kept on site under administrator control. Staff check storage monthly and document any concern, without reading the resident's private items.

Staff obtain each new prescription from the contracted pharmacy within 48 hours of the order. Staff update the MAR within 48 hours of the new order. Staff document the date and time of the order and the date the MAR was updated.

Staff receive medications in original containers or pharmacy unit-dose or multi-dose packaging. The receiving staff member checks label against order, counts controlled substances with a second staff member, and records receipt. Medications are never transferred to unlabeled containers.

All medications are stored under lock and key. Controlled substances are stored in a locked cabinet or box of substantial construction, separate from other medications. A log is updated daily showing each dose removed and each shift count. Two staff reconcile the count at each shift change and sign. A discrepancy is reported to the administrator immediately and investigated the same day.
The administrator controls access to keys and keeps a duplicate set on site in a secure location. A list of key holders is kept, and keys are never taken off the premises or left unattended.

Only trained staff perform the assistance tasks the rules allow. Staff must have completed medication-assistance training under PCH-03 and had a competency check before doing any task. The Home does not allow staff to administer medications unless they are CMAs. Before relying on a CMA, the administrator checks the Georgia Certified Medication Aide Registry, records the check date, and re-checks it at least annually.

If a resident has a prescribed epinephrine auto-injector, the prescriber provides a written protocol. Trained staff may use the EpiPen under that protocol, call 911 immediately, notify the representative, and complete an incident report under PCH-08.

Staff record every dose on the MAR daily at the time it is taken or assisted with. Refusals, omissions, holds and PRN use (with reason and result) are recorded. Staff notify the prescriber of repeated refusals or errors the same day and the administrator of any error immediately.

If a medication error, adverse reaction or missed dose occurs, staff check the resident, call the prescriber or pharmacist for direction, call 911 if there is any risk to life, notify the representative or legal surrogate, and record the event in the resident file. The administrator investigates the cause and records corrective action in the central QA file (see PCH-08, PCH-11).

[CONSULTANT PHARMACIST NAME] performs a drug regimen review for each resident quarterly. The administrator gives recommendations to the prescriber within 5 business days and records the response in the resident file.

[RN NAME], RN, or the consultant pharmacist observes staff performing medication tasks on a random basis at least quarterly and documents the observation. The administrator ensures staff skills competency is checked at hire and annually. Staff who fail the check are removed from medication tasks until retrained and re-checked.

For hospice residents, the Home accepts and stores liquid morphine up to the 50 ml limit per hospice patient. The Home logs it as a controlled substance and coordinates with the hospice on handling and disposal (see HLT-04).

The Home disposes of discontinued, expired or deceased residents' medications following FDA and EPA guidance. Two staff witness the disposal. Staff record the medication, quantity, date, method and both signatures. Controlled substances are destroyed only with a witness and are logged.

The administrator reviews MARs, controlled substance logs, storage checks, and drug regimen review follow-up at least monthly. The administrator summarizes findings for the quarterly QA review and updates this policy whenever the rules change.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, decides whether the Home will use CMAs, and funds pharmacist and RN oversight.
Keeps orders and the MAR current, controls keys, verifies CMA registry status, investigates errors, and reviews logs monthly.
Performs quarterly drug regimen reviews, advises on storage and disposal, and may perform quarterly random observations.
Performs quarterly random observations, annual competency reviews and oversight for staff who assist with medications.
Perform only the tasks they are trained and permitted to do, document every dose, and report errors immediately.
Provides orders for all medications, including OTC, and responds to pharmacist recommendations.

documentation: Prescriber orders for every medication including OTC
Daily MAR with the 48-hour new-order update dates
Controlled substance log with shift counts
Medication receipt and disposal records with witness signatures
Self-administration assessments in care plans
CMA registry verification dates
Competency checks, quarterly random observation records and annual competency reviews
Quarterly drug regimen review reports and prescriber responses
Medication error reports and QA file entries
EpiPen protocols and key holder list

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Health and Hygiene: Infection Control, Work and Return-to-Work, Foodborne Illness, Reportable Diseases
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Home (PCH, 2–24 beds): all staff, volunteers, proxy caregivers, food handlers and the administrator
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents, staff and visitors at [AGENCY NAME] (the "Home"). It also sets clear rules for when ill staff stay home and return to work, how foodborne illness is handled, and how reportable diseases are reported.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(h), "Health and hygiene issues for residents and staff relating to infection control, work policies and return to work policies, food borne illnesses and reportable diseases." The governing body has adopted it under 111-8-62-.07. Under it, the Home (1) applies standard precautions and hand hygiene at all times for infection control; (2) requires every employee to have a TB screening and physical within the 12 months before providing care, following the Georgia standard in 111-8-63-.09(10), and the administrator confirms the matching Ch. 111-8-62 paragraph; (3) sets written work-exclusion and return-to-work criteria below; (4) keeps perishable food at or below 41 degrees F, and isolates residents and reports when foodborne illness is suspected; and (5) reports reportable diseases to the local health district as the Georgia Department of Public Health requires. The Home follows OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 for exposure to blood and bodily fluids. The Home does not allow any staff member with an infectious illness to give care or handle food while contagious.

definitions.definition: Infection-control practices applied to every resident regardless of diagnosis, including hand hygiene, gloves and other protective equipment, respiratory etiquette, and safe sharps and waste handling.
Requiring an ill staff member, volunteer or visitor to stay away from residents and food until the return-to-work criteria are met.
A disease or condition that Georgia Department of Public Health rules require be reported to the local health district.
Two or more residents or staff with the same or similar illness in the same time period, or any illness cluster the health district identifies as an outbreak.
Contact of the eyes, mouth, mucous membranes or non-intact skin with blood or other potentially infectious material.

procedures: Before a new employee gives care, the administrator verifies a TB screening and a physical completed within the previous 12 months. The administrator files the results in the personnel file (see STF-02). A person with a positive screen is not placed with residents until medically cleared in writing. Employees repeat screening as required by the health district and the Home's employee health plan.

All staff are trained on standard precautions, hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, glove and personal protective equipment (PPE) use, and the OSHA bloodborne pathogen standard at orientation and at least annually. Attendance is recorded under PCH-03.

Staff wash hands or use alcohol-based hand rub before and after resident care, before handling food or medications, after toileting or bathroom assistance, after removing gloves, and when visibly soiled. The Home keeps soap, paper towels, hand rub, gloves and PPE stocked at all points of care. The on-site manager checks supplies weekly.

Staff place used sharps in puncture-resistant containers at the point of use and never recap needles. Contaminated waste is bagged and removed per the bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan. The Home offers the hepatitis B vaccine to staff with reasonably anticipated exposure within 10 working days of assignment.

After an exposure incident, the staff member washes the area immediately, reports to the administrator right away, and is sent for medical evaluation. The administrator records the incident and follow-up confidentially.

Staff report to the administrator or on-site manager before a shift if they have fever, vomiting, diarrhea, undiagnosed rash, jaundice, a sore throat with fever, a draining or infected wound that cannot be covered, or a diagnosed communicable illness. The administrator excludes the staff member from resident care and food handling.

Return-to-work criteria: a staff member may return when fever-free for 24 hours without fever-reducing medication, and when free of vomiting and diarrhea for 48 hours. A staff member with a diagnosed communicable illness returns when the health care provider or health district clears the person. The administrator documents the exclusion dates and return approval in the personnel file.

Residents with signs of infection are assessed by staff, and the resident's physician and representative are notified the same day (see HLT-01). The Home uses private rooms or other reasonable separation when necessary to limit spread. Staff use PPE as appropriate and record the illness and response in the resident file.

Cold perishable food is kept at or below 41 degrees F. Staff check refrigerator and freezer temperatures at least daily and record them on a log. Food held outside the safe range, or past its date, is discarded and the event is noted. Food handlers wear clean clothing, restrain hair, and do not prepare food while ill (see DL-01).

When two or more residents or staff have vomiting, diarrhea or other symptoms suggestive of foodborne illness, the on-site manager (1) separates ill residents from others where practical, (2) saves any suspect food and records the menu, (3) assures fluids and obtains medical attention, (4) notifies the administrator immediately, and (5) calls the local health district for guidance the same day.

The administrator notifies residents' representatives of an outbreak and of any restrictions on visiting. The administrator records the outbreak, actions taken and the health district's instructions. If the illness leads to serious injury requiring medical attention, an unanticipated death, or an event affecting safe operation, the administrator also reports to DCH within 24 hours under PCH-08.

The administrator keeps a current list of Georgia reportable diseases and the local health district contact number. When a physician, laboratory or staff diagnoses a reportable disease or suspected outbreak, the administrator reports to the local health district within the timeframe the Department of Public Health requires, and records the date, time and name of the person who took the report.

Housekeeping and laundry follow written routines: high-touch surfaces are cleaned and disinfected daily and after any soiling; soiled linen is handled with gloves, bagged at the point of use and washed hot with detergent; and clean and soiled linen are stored separately (see DL-03).

The Home encourages and offers residents and staff vaccinations such as influenza and pneumococcal, according to the resident's physician orders and personal choice. Staff record offers and declinations.
The administrator reviews infection data (illness logs, exclusions, outbreaks) every quarter in the QA review and records any changes to practice in the central QA file (see PCH-11).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy and provides the supplies, training and access to medical evaluation needed to carry it out.
Verifies TB screenings and physicals, excludes ill staff, directs outbreak response, makes health district and DCH reports, and keeps logs.
Follow standard precautions, report their own illness before a shift, and report resident illness promptly.
Maintain safe food temperatures, record logs and stay out of food preparation while ill.
Evaluates ill residents and gives treatment orders and reporting information.

documentation: TB screening and physical results in each personnel file
Employee illness, exclusion and return-to-work records
Hepatitis B vaccine offers, declinations and exposure incident records
Refrigerator and freezer temperature logs
Resident illness records and outbreak logs
Health district and DCH report records
Infection control and bloodborne pathogen training attendance
Quarterly QA infection review notes

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Investigation and Reporting of Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation, Wandering, Accidents, Injuries and Changes in Condition
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Home (PCH, 2–24 beds): all staff, volunteers, proxy caregivers, administrator and governing body
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] (the "Home") responds at once to abuse, neglect, exploitation, a missing resident, an accident, an injury, a death or a change in a resident's condition. It requires prompt investigation and reporting to the people and agencies Georgia requires.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(i), "The investigation and reporting of abuse, neglect, exploitation of residents, residents' wandering away from the community, accidents, injuries and changes in residents' conditions to required parties." The governing body has adopted it under 111-8-62-.07. The Home uses the Georgia assisted living reporting standard (111-8-63-.30 and 111-8-63-.26) as its operating standard, and the administrator confirms the matching Ch. 111-8-62 paragraphs against the current rule text. On an accident or sudden adverse change in condition, staff act immediately, notify the representative or legal surrogate, and record the change and response in the resident file. The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of any accident, injury or death. The Home calls local police within 30 minutes of actual knowledge that a resident is missing and reports the start and end of a Mattie's Call to DCH within 30 minutes of the contact with law enforcement. The Home reports serious incidents to DCH within 24 hours of the incident or of reasonable cause to believe one occurred. Abuse, neglect and exploitation are reported under the Long-Term Care Facility Resident Abuse Reporting Act. Copies of investigation records go in the resident file and a central quality-assurance (QA) file.

definitions.definition: An accidental or unanticipated death not tied to the natural course of illness; a serious injury needing medical attention; rape, assault, battery, abuse, neglect or exploitation; an external disaster or emergency affecting safe operation; or an owner, director or employee acquiring a criminal record.
The Georgia statewide alert for a missing person. The Home reports its start and end to DCH.
A sudden or significant change in a resident's physical, mental or functional status, including any accident or injury.
Harm to or misuse of a resident, as defined in Ch. 111-8-62 and the Long-Term Care Facility Resident Abuse Reporting Act, including misuse of a resident's money or property.
The Home's single file of incident investigations and reports used for quarterly quality review.

procedures: Any staff member, volunteer or proxy caregiver who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation protects the resident first, then tells the administrator or on-site manager immediately. If a resident is in danger, staff call 911. A staff member may also report directly to DCH or the other agencies named in the Act, and the Home never discourages or punishes such a report.

On an accident or sudden adverse change, the nearest trained staff assess the resident, give first aid, and call 911 if there is any life-threatening concern. Staff stay with the resident and keep emergency numbers and the resident's information (face sheet, medication list, advance directive) ready, including during transport (see HLT-01).

If a resident is unresponsive: for a hospice enrollee, call the hospice first, then the health care agent, then EMS with CPR if no DNR. If a valid DNR order exists, honor it in good faith. If there is a health care agent (O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq.), call the agent, and if the agent is unavailable and there is no DNR, call EMS and start CPR. If there is no hospice, DNR or directive, call EMS and start CPR unless clearly futile and no physician, authorized RN or PA is on site.

Staff notify the representative or legal surrogate as soon as the resident is safe, and record who was notified, when and by whom. Staff record the change and the response in the resident file the same shift.

When a resident is missing, staff immediately search the building and grounds under the SAF-01 plan. Within 30 minutes of actual knowledge that a resident is missing, the administrator or on-site manager calls local police. The staff member records the time the resident was found missing and the time police were called.

Within 30 minutes of the contact with law enforcement about a missing resident, the administrator or on-site manager reports the start of the Mattie's Call to DCH. When the resident is found, the Home reports the end of the Mattie's Call to DCH within 30 minutes of the contact with law enforcement. The Home notifies the representative and ensures a medical check after return (see SAF-01).

The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of every accident, injury or death. The investigator interviews involved staff and witnesses, reviews the scene, equipment and care plan, and secures evidence. The investigation starts the same day.

For suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the administrator immediately removes the accused person from resident contact and from any assigned duties involving the resident until the investigation is completed (see PCH-09). The administrator separates the resident from any alleged abuser and arranges medical care and emotional support.

The administrator reports serious incidents to DCH within 24 hours of the incident or of reasonable cause to believe one occurred. The report states the Home's and administrator's names, the date of the incident and date of discovery, the type of incident with a brief description, and the immediate corrective or preventive action taken. The administrator keeps proof of submission.

The administrator reports suspected abuse, neglect and exploitation under the Long-Term Care Facility Resident Abuse Reporting Act, and also calls law enforcement for any suspected crime. The administrator also reports to DCH within 24 hours as a serious incident. An owner, director or employee who acquires a criminal record is reported to DCH within 24 hours of the Home learning of it (see STF-01).
Staff and administrator report an external disaster or emergency affecting safe operation to DCH within 24 hours, and follow PCH-10 for relocation notices.

The administrator reports the investigation results to the representative or legal surrogate and gives the resident a plain-language explanation. The administrator files copies of the investigation and report in the resident file and in the central QA file within 5 business days of the incident, and updates them when the outcome is final.

The administrator updates the resident's care plan and reassesses the resident after any accident, injury or change in condition (see ADM-02). The administrator notifies the physician of the change the same day (see HLT-01).

The administrator reviews all incidents each month for patterns such as repeat falls, locations, shifts or staff involved, and takes corrective action. Findings feed the quarterly QA review (see PCH-11).

The administrator trains all staff at orientation and annually on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect, exploitation and wandering, and on the 24-hour and 30-minute deadlines. The administrator keeps a copy of the DCH reporting contacts in the office and at the on-site manager's station.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, reviews quarterly incident trends, and ensures the administrator has resources to investigate and report.
Leads investigations, makes police and DCH reports on time, notifies representatives, protects residents and files all records.

responsibilities.role: All staff, volunteers and proxy caregivers
responsibilities.duty: Report immediately any suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation, missing resident, accident, injury or change in condition.
Is notified of changes in condition and gives treatment direction.
Is notified promptly and receives the investigation result.

documentation: Incident, accident and change-in-condition reports in the resident file
Investigation notes, witness statements and corrective action records
Copies of DCH serious incident reports with submission proof
Mattie's Call start and end reports with police contact times
Representative notification records
Central QA file entries
Abuse reporting training attendance records
Monthly incident trend summaries

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Staff Discipline for Conduct Inconsistent With Home Policies
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Home (PCH, 2–24 beds): all employees, supervisors, administrator and governing body
policies.purpose: To set fair, consistent and documented steps for handling staff conduct that violates the policies of [AGENCY NAME] (the "Home"), while protecting residents first.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(j), "Discipline procedures for handling conduct which is inconsistent with the policies of the home committed by staff." The governing body has adopted it under 111-8-62-.07. The Home uses progressive discipline for ordinary violations, and skips steps when a violation is serious or puts residents at risk. Any staff member accused of abuse, neglect or exploitation is removed immediately from resident contact while the Home investigates. Staff may not work while impaired by alcohol, drugs or any other cause (following the standard in 111-8-63-.09(17)). Staff may not coerce or pressure a resident to assign money, valuables or property to the Home or to any staff member. When an owner, director or employee acquires a criminal record, the Home reports it to DCH within 24 hours (following 111-8-63-.30). All disciplinary action is documented in the personnel file. The Home never retaliates against any staff member who reports a concern in good faith.

definitions.definition: A sequence of responses that increases with the seriousness or repetition of the violation: verbal warning, written warning, final written warning or suspension, and termination.

Conduct that may cause harm to a resident or the Home, including abuse, neglect, exploitation, theft, working while impaired, falsifying records, breach of confidentiality, or ignoring a resident's call for help.
Suspension from direct care and from any contact with residents, with or without pay as the Home determines, pending an investigation.
Being under the influence of alcohol, illegal drugs, misused medication or any condition that affects the ability to give safe care.

procedures: At hire, each employee receives the Home's policies and conduct standards and signs an acknowledgment. The administrator files the signed acknowledgment in the personnel file (see STF-02).

A supervisor who observes or learns of conduct inconsistent with Home policy tells the administrator the same day. If the conduct involves resident safety, the supervisor acts immediately to protect residents.

For allegations of abuse, neglect or exploitation, the administrator removes the accused staff member from resident contact immediately, before the investigation starts. The administrator investigates under PCH-08 and makes any required report to DCH within 24 hours and to other agencies under the Long-Term Care Facility Resident Abuse Reporting Act.

The administrator gathers facts within 3 business days for non-emergency matters. The administrator interviews the employee and witnesses, reviews records, and gives the employee a chance to explain. The administrator records the findings in writing.
For first or minor violations (for example, lateness or minor documentation errors), the supervisor gives a documented verbal warning and records the date, policy, facts and expected improvement.

For repeated or more significant violations, the administrator issues a written warning. It states the policy violated, the facts, required corrective action, a deadline for improvement and the consequence of further violations. The employee is asked to sign. If the employee refuses, the administrator notes the refusal.

For continued violations or a serious violation, the administrator may issue a final written warning, suspend the employee, or terminate employment. The administrator may skip earlier steps for serious misconduct.

A staff member suspected of working while impaired is removed from duty at once, and the administrator arranges safe transportation home. The administrator documents the observations and requires testing or medical evaluation as the Home's written policy allows. A confirmed violation leads to discipline up to termination.

If a staff member is found to have asked, pressured or accepted money, valuables or property from a resident in violation of resident rights, the administrator treats it as suspected exploitation, removes the staff member from resident contact, reports under PCH-08, and returns any item to the resident or representative (see RR-03).

When the administrator learns an owner, director or employee has acquired a criminal record, the administrator reports it to DCH within 24 hours and evaluates the person's role and continued access to residents. Where a background check or registry result affects eligibility, the administrator follows STF-01.
Staff who report violations or participate in investigations are protected from retaliation. Any adverse treatment of such a person is itself treated as serious misconduct.

Every disciplinary action is written, dated, reviewed with the employee, and filed in the personnel file within 2 business days. The Home keeps personnel files for at least 3 years after the employee leaves.

Employees may submit a written response to any disciplinary record, and the administrator places it in the personnel file. The employee may ask the governing body chair to review a termination within 5 business days.

The administrator reports to the governing body at least quarterly on the number and type of disciplinary actions, without unnecessary identifying details, and uses the pattern to adjust training (see PCH-03, PCH-11).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts this policy, reviews quarterly disciplinary summaries, and hears termination review requests.
Investigates, decides on discipline, removes staff from resident contact when needed, makes DCH reports and keeps records.
Report conduct problems the same day, give verbal warnings, and protect residents.
Follow Home policies, report violations, and cooperate with investigations.

documentation: Signed policy acknowledgments
Verbal and written warnings, suspension and termination records in the personnel file
Investigation notes and findings
Records of removal from resident contact and return dates
Impairment observation records
DCH reports concerning employee criminal records
Employee written responses and review requests
Quarterly disciplinary summaries to the governing body

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Emergency Preparedness, Drills and Evacuation
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Home (PCH, 2–24 beds): all staff, volunteers, residents, administrator and governing body
policies.purpose: To prepare [AGENCY NAME] (the "Home"), its staff and its residents to respond safely to fire, severe weather, power loss, medical emergencies and other disasters, and to evacuate or relocate residents when necessary.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(k), "Emergency preparedness, drills and evacuation requirements." The governing body has adopted it under 111-8-62-.07. The Home maintains a written disaster plan that complies with Ch. 111-8-16 (Disaster Preparedness Plans). The plan is readily accessible to staff, residents and families, and it names the staff positions responsible for carrying it out and for obtaining emergency medical attention. Evacuation maps with marked escape routes are posted on each floor, and a clear accessible emergency route is kept through common areas. The Home documents fire and evacuation drills at the frequency required by the State Fire Marshal and DCH. If an emergency forces relocation, the Home gives timely notice of the relocation address to residents, family contacts, representatives and DCH. Emergency contact numbers and each resident's information are kept ready for use and for transport. The Home's policies are available for review at DCH's unannounced inspections.

definitions.definition: The Home's written plan under Ch. 111-8-16 for emergencies such as fire, tornado, flood, severe weather, loss of utilities, infectious outbreak and evacuation.
A posted floor plan showing the viewer's location, exits and marked escape routes.
Moving residents out of the Home, temporarily or permanently, because an emergency makes it unsafe to stay.
A job title named in the disaster plan (for example, administrator, on-site manager, shift lead) that carries out defined duties during an emergency.

procedures: The administrator writes the disaster plan under Ch. 111-8-16, covering fire, tornado and severe weather, flood, power or water loss, medical emergencies, bomb threat, infectious disease outbreak, missing resident, and evacuation and relocation. The governing body reviews and approves the plan at adoption and at least annually.

The plan names by position who is in charge on each shift, who calls 911 and obtains emergency medical attention, who accounts for residents, who shuts off utilities, who contacts families and DCH, and who relays information to responders. Each position has a named backup, listed by title and current name.

The administrator keeps the plan at the front office and in a binder at the on-site manager's station, and gives a summary at admission to each resident and representative. Residents and families may read or receive a copy on request.

The administrator posts evacuation maps with marked escape routes on every floor, near exits and stairways, and updates them within 5 business days of any layout change. Staff check postings monthly during safety rounds.
Staff keep exits, hallways, stairways and common areas clear of obstructions. A clear, accessible emergency route through the common areas is checked daily and recorded on the safety checklist.

The administrator keeps an emergency contact list at the on-site manager's station. It includes 911, the fire department, utilities, DCH, each resident's physician, each representative, the pharmacy, backup transportation and the receiving facility. It is reviewed monthly and updated as information changes.

The administrator keeps for each resident a grab-and-go emergency record containing the face sheet, medication list, allergies, diagnoses, advance directive or DNR, representative contact, and mobility needs. It is available at all times and goes with the resident during any transport. The record is updated at each care plan review and after any change.

Staff drill the fire response and evacuation. The administrator confirms with the State Fire Marshal and DCH the required drill frequency for the Home and records it in the drill log. Until the required frequency is confirmed in writing, the Home conducts at least one fire and evacuation drill every quarter on each shift, including nights, and varies the time and scenario.

After each drill, the on-site manager documents the date, time, shift, type of drill, number of staff and residents involved, time to evacuate, problems found, and corrective action. The administrator reviews the record within 3 business days and signs it.

New staff learn the disaster plan, their responsibilities, evacuation routes, fire extinguisher use and resident evacuation techniques during orientation, before working alone with residents. All staff review the plan at least annually. Attendance is recorded under PCH-03.

During a real emergency, the on-site manager takes charge until the administrator arrives, calls 911 as needed, accounts for every resident by roster, moves residents to safety, and keeps the roster, medications and emergency records with the group. Staff do not leave until all residents are accounted for.

If emergency conditions require relocation, the administrator selects the receiving site named in the disaster plan, arranges transportation, medications and records, and keeps residents together where practical. The administrator gives timely notice of the relocation address to residents, family contacts, representatives and DCH as soon as it is known.
The administrator reports an external disaster or emergency affecting safe operation to DCH within 24 hours of the event, giving the information listed in PCH-08.

Staff provide for residents' medical needs during the emergency. They continue medications, keep the emergency record with each resident, and document any care provided and any resident harmed. Where possible, residents on oxygen or other medical equipment have backup supplies under the plan.

The administrator holds a review after every real emergency and every drill that exposes problems. The administrator revises the plan if needed and records the review in the central QA file (see PCH-11). The administrator also keeps current fire safety documents, such as the State Fire Marshal report and electrical compliance records, available for DCH inspection (see SAF-03, GOV-01).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the disaster plan, reviews it at least annually, and provides funds for supplies, equipment and training.
Writes and updates the plan, schedules drills, trains staff, notifies DCH, and keeps emergency records and drill logs.
Takes charge in an emergency, accounts for residents, directs evacuation and keeps the emergency contact list and records ready.
Know their roles and routes, take part in drills, and keep escape routes clear.
Are informed of the plan and told the relocation address if the Home must relocate.

documentation: Written disaster plan with annual governing body approval
Posted evacuation maps and monthly posting checks
Fire and evacuation drill logs with corrective actions
Emergency contact list and resident grab-and-go emergency records
Staff orientation and annual emergency training attendance
Relocation notices to residents, families, representatives and DCH
DCH 24-hour report for any external disaster or emergency
Post-emergency and post-drill review notes in the central QA file
State Fire Marshal report and electrical compliance records

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Quality Assurance and Peer Review Using Serious Incident Reports and Feedback
policies.applies_to: PCH
policies.purpose: To give [AGENCY NAME] a scheduled, documented way to learn from serious incidents, investigations, resident and family feedback and inspection results, and to turn what it learns into better care for residents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates a quality assurance (QA) and peer review program. The program uses reports and investigations of serious incidents, together with resident and family feedback, to find opportunities to improve care. This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(l) (PCH .07(3)(l)): Quality assurance and peer review mechanisms to determine opportunities for improving care utilizing information acquired from reports and investigations of serious incidents, including resident and family feedback. The governing body is responsible for the program. The administrator or on-site manager runs it day to day. The home keeps a central QA file. This follows the central-file practice that the ALC change-in-condition rule requires, which we adopt as good practice for the PCH. QA findings are used to improve care. They are not used to punish people for good-faith reporting.

definitions.definition: An event that causes or could cause significant harm to a resident. Examples: abuse, neglect or exploitation; an elopement or wandering event; a fall with injury; an unexplained injury; a hospital transfer after an accident; a death; a significant medication error; a resident-to-resident altercation; a fire or other emergency that affects residents.
One confidential file, kept by the administrator, that holds copies of incident reports, investigations, QA meeting minutes, corrective action logs, feedback summaries and inspection results.

A structured review of a care practice or event (for example a medication error, a fall or a discharge) by staff and professionals who did not take part in the event. It looks at the process, not at assigning blame.
A specific, dated step, with a named person responsible, taken to fix a problem or reduce the chance it happens again.

procedures: The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of any accident, injury or death, as described in PCH-08. Staff who witnessed the event complete a written incident report before the end of their shift.

The administrator or on-site manager reports the event to the resident's representative or legal surrogate and records the notice and the home's response in the resident's record. A copy of the incident report and investigation goes into the resident file and into the central QA file.

The administrator opens a QA entry in the central QA file for every serious incident. The entry gives the date, the event type, the people involved, the investigation findings and any report made to outside agencies.

The QA review team meets at least quarterly. The administrator or on-site manager leads it. Members are the person in charge of medications, a direct care staff representative, the consulting pharmacist or nurse where the home uses one, and an owner or governing body representative. The team meets sooner after any death, abuse allegation, serious injury or elopement.

At each meeting the team reviews all serious incident reports and investigations since the last meeting. It looks for patterns by resident, by shift, by location, by staff member and by type of event.

The team carries out peer review of medication errors, falls, hospital transfers, discharges and any other event the administrator selects. The review asks what happened, why, whether staff followed policy and the care plan, and what should change.

For every problem found, the team records a corrective action with a responsible person and a due date. Examples: staff retraining, care plan revisions, environmental changes, staffing changes, policy changes.
The administrator reviews each open corrective action at every meeting. Actions are closed only when the administrator notes in the file the date and the proof of completion.

The home collects resident and family feedback in at least four ways: (a) a written satisfaction survey given to each resident and representative at least annually; (b) a resident meeting at least quarterly; (c) a suggestion box or form kept in a common area; and (d) a documented conversation with each family at least annually and after any serious incident. Residents may give feedback anonymously. Grievances follow RR-01.
The administrator logs all feedback, summarizes it for each QA meeting, and records what the home did in response. The home tells residents and families what changed, through meetings or postings.

The team reviews every DCH inspection report and plan of correction at the first QA meeting after the report is received. It checks that each plan-of-correction action was done on time and holds up. The review is also recorded in the central QA file.

The team reviews resident-specific trends (falls, weight loss, skin problems, behavior changes). It confirms that the resident's care plan was revised and the physician was told where needed (see HLT-01 and ADM-02).

The administrator gives the governing body a written QA summary at least quarterly. It covers the number and type of incidents, trends, corrective actions, feedback themes and inspection results. The governing body records its review and any direction in its minutes.

The administrator keeps QA records confidential and shares them only with the governing body, DCH or other persons as the law requires. No resident or staff member is retaliated against for reporting a concern or giving feedback.
The administrator reviews this policy annually, as part of the annual manual review in GOV-02, and updates it when QA results show the program is not working.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees the QA program, reviews the quarterly summary, records its direction, and makes resources available for corrective actions.
Runs the QA program, investigates incidents, maintains the central QA file, leads the QA team and tracks corrective actions to completion.
Reviews incidents, performs peer review, reviews feedback and inspection results, and assigns corrective actions.
Report incidents and concerns right away, complete incident reports before the end of shift, and take part in corrective training.
Gives clinical input on medication errors, falls and other care events reviewed by the team.

documentation: Incident reports and investigation reports (copy in resident file and in central QA file)
Central QA file, with quarterly QA meeting minutes and sign-in sheets
Peer review notes for medication errors, falls, discharges and other selected events
Corrective action log with responsible person, due date and completion date
Resident and family survey forms, resident meeting minutes, suggestion forms and feedback log
Inspection reports, plans of correction and QA review notes
Quarterly QA summary to the governing body and governing body minutes

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Volunteers With Unsupervised Access and Proxy Caregivers
policies.applies_to: PCH
policies.purpose: To set the conditions under which [AGENCY NAME] allows volunteers to have unsupervised access to residents, to make sure they are oriented to resident rights and basic safety precautions, and to state how proxy caregivers are used and overseen.
policies.policy: This policy meets two items of Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3). PCH .07(3)(m): The use of volunteers, who have unsupervised access to the residents and their orientation regarding resident's rights and basic safety precautions. PCH .07(3)(n): The specific use of proxy caregivers allowed within the home and the oversight of proxy caregivers the home requires or provides in accordance with Georgia law, these rules and the rules for proxy caregivers, Chapter 111-8-100. Volunteers may have unsupervised access to residents only after screening, approval by the administrator and orientation. Volunteers never count toward required staffing and never perform medication tasks. [AGENCY NAME] permits proxy caregivers only when the resident or the resident's representative requests it in writing, the administrator approves it, and the requirements of Chapter 111-8-100 are met. The home does not assign its own employees to act as proxy caregivers.

definitions.definition: A person who gives time to the home or its residents without pay and is not an employee, contractor, family member visiting their own relative, or proxy caregiver.
Time alone with one or more residents, or in a resident's room or private space, when a staff member is not in direct sight or presence.
A person who is not employed by the home and who is designated, as permitted by Georgia law and Chapter 111-8-100, to perform certain health maintenance activities for a resident.
The home's current list of approved volunteers and designated proxy caregivers.

procedures: Anyone who wants to volunteer completes a volunteer application. It gives name, contact information, the activity they propose and a statement that they understand the confidentiality and resident rights rules.

The administrator interviews the applicant and decides in writing whether the person may volunteer and whether the person may have unsupervised access. Volunteers who are not cleared for unsupervised access are always accompanied by a staff member.

Before any unsupervised access, the administrator completes the screening for the person. This includes checking photo identification and a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry (see PCH-13). It also includes the background check required by DCH rules for volunteers with unsupervised access. The administrator confirms the current requirement with DCH ([PHONE] on the DCH contact sheet in GOV-02) and records the date of the confirmation in the volunteer file. Anyone who has not cleared is not given unsupervised access.

Every volunteer receives written and verbal orientation before the first shift. It covers: resident rights (PCH-05); privacy and confidentiality (RR-05); recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation (PCH-08); fire and emergency procedures (PCH-10); hand hygiene and illness rules (PCH-07); wandering and elopement precautions; safe transfers and what the volunteer may not do; and who to tell about concerns. The volunteer signs and dates an orientation acknowledgment.

Volunteers do not give medications or assist with self-administration, do not provide personal care such as bathing, toileting or transferring, do not handle resident money or valuables, and do not transport residents unless the administrator has approved the driver and vehicle. Volunteers are not counted in the staffing plan in PCH-14.
Volunteers wear a visible volunteer badge, sign in and out at the front desk, and stay in the areas they are assigned.
A staff member is assigned to be the volunteer's contact for each shift. Volunteers report any injury, incident, unusual behavior or resident complaint to that person immediately.

The administrator may end a volunteer's access at any time and must do so right away if the volunteer breaks a resident right, violates a house rule or is the subject of an abuse, neglect or exploitation allegation. Any allegation is reported under PCH-08.

The administrator keeps a volunteer roster showing name, contact information, date cleared, type of access (supervised or unsupervised), orientation date and end date. The roster is reviewed at least quarterly.

The home's position on proxy caregivers is as follows. A resident or representative who wants a proxy caregiver submits a written request naming the person and the activities. The administrator reviews the request against Chapter 111-8-100 and the resident's assessment and care plan, then approves or denies it in writing, giving reasons if denied.

Before the proxy caregiver acts, the administrator confirms that all requirements of Chapter 111-8-100 are met. These include the written designation, instruction by the licensed health professional the chapter requires, and any record the chapter requires. Copies go in the resident's record.

The home's oversight of a proxy caregiver includes: confirming the proxy caregiver's identity and clearance (see PCH-13); having the proxy caregiver sign in and out; having the administrator or on-site manager check at least monthly that the proxy caregiver is performing only the approved activities, that records are complete and that the resident is safe; and recording the check in the resident's record.

Proxy caregivers are told that they may not perform tasks beyond their designation, and that they must follow the home's rules on resident rights, privacy, infection control and emergencies. They are also told they must report any change in the resident's condition, medication problem or incident to the on-site manager at once.

The administrator may suspend or end a proxy caregiver's access if the proxy caregiver does not follow the designation, creates a risk to a resident or breaks a rule. The home informs the resident or representative promptly and revises the care plan. If the resident was harmed, the event is investigated and reported under PCH-08.
The home never allows a volunteer or proxy caregiver to replace required staff and never relies on either to cover an absence.

responsibilities.duty: Screens and approves volunteers and proxy caregivers, confirms the current background-check requirement with DCH, keeps the roster, and provides orientation and oversight.
Act as the volunteer's contact, monitor volunteers and proxy caregivers during the shift, stop unsafe activity and report concerns.
Complete orientation, stay within assigned duties, protect resident privacy and report concerns right away.
Perform only the designated activities in the way Chapter 111-8-100 and the home require, and report changes in the resident's condition.
Approves the home's position on proxy caregivers and reviews this policy annually.

documentation: Volunteer application, approval and clearance documentation
Signed volunteer orientation acknowledgment
Volunteer and proxy caregiver roster
Volunteer and proxy caregiver sign-in logs
DCH confirmation note on the volunteer background check requirement
Written proxy caregiver request, administrator approval or denial and the designation records required by Chapter 111-8-100
Monthly oversight notes for proxy caregivers in the resident record

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Safety and Security Precautions Against Harm by Other Residents, Proxy Caregivers and Outside Individuals
policies.applies_to: PCH
policies.purpose: To protect residents from harm by other residents, designated proxy caregivers and other people who are not employed by [AGENCY NAME] but routinely come into the home.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(o) (PCH .07(3)(o)): The safety and security precautions that will be employed by the home to protect residents from harm by other residents, designated proxy caregivers and other individuals, not employed by the home who routinely come into the home. The home screens applicants before admission, controls who enters the building, identifies staff and visitors, screens outside people who routinely come in (such as hospice and home health staff), and has a set response to any resident-to-resident incident. The home follows the admission screening model of the ALC admission rule (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.15(2)): the administrator or on-site manager documents the evaluation of each applicant, including a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry or a fingerprint check, and documents added safety measures for registered sex offenders or violent offenders. The administrator will confirm the PCH paragraph on this point with DCH and update this policy if the PCH rule differs.

definitions.term: Outside individual who routinely comes into the home
definitions.definition: A person not employed by the home who comes in on a regular basis. Examples: hospice, home health and therapy staff, a visiting physician or nurse, a barber, a pharmacy delivery person, a vendor, a clergy member and a private caregiver.

Specific protective steps recorded in the care plan or admission file for a resident with a history of sexual offenses or violence. Examples: room location, supervision level, restrictions on being alone with other residents, door and night checks.
Any physical, verbal, sexual or other unwanted contact or conduct between residents that causes or could cause harm or distress.

procedures: Before admission, the administrator or on-site manager documents an evaluation of the applicant under ADM-01. The evaluation includes a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry (or a fingerprint check where the home uses one) and a review of any history the applicant, family or referral source discloses of violence, aggression or sexual offenses. The result, the date and the name of the person who ran it go in the admission file.

If the applicant is a registered sex offender or has a history of violence, the administrator decides, with the physician or referral source where possible, whether the home can safely serve the person. If admitted, the administrator writes specific added safety measures into the care plan. Examples: a room away from vulnerable residents, a supervision level, no unsupervised contact with named residents, and increased night checks. The administrator tells the resident's representative about the measures as the law permits and reviews them at every reassessment. If the home cannot keep other residents safe, it declines the admission.

The home keeps the front door locked or monitored at all times and controls entry in a way that does not trap residents or violate fire safety requirements (SAF-03). Staff greet each visitor and ask who they are visiting.

Every visitor, vendor and contractor signs a visitor log at entry and exit with name, date, time in and out, and the resident or purpose of the visit. Staff do not let anyone take a resident off the premises unless the resident or representative has approved it and the departure is logged.
Staff, including the administrator, wear photo or name identification badges while on duty. Volunteers and proxy caregivers wear badges that show their role.

Outside individuals who routinely come in, such as hospice and home health staff, are screened before their first visit. The on-site manager confirms the name of the agency, the person's identity, that the agency is licensed where licensure is required, and that the person is expected by the resident. The agency is asked to confirm its own background screening of its employees, and this is recorded. The person signs in, wears the agency badge and may only be with the residents they serve.
Proxy caregivers are screened as described in PCH-12 before they act. They sign in at each visit, may only be with the resident they were designated for, and are monitored monthly.

Staff do not leave visitors or outside individuals alone with residents they are not assigned to see. Staff may ask any visitor to leave who is disruptive, appears impaired or threatens a resident. The administrator may bar a visitor in writing where the resident's safety requires it, while respecting resident rights (PCH-05).
