Staff supervise common areas and watch for residents who show aggression, wandering into others' rooms, sexual behavior toward others, or who are afraid of another resident. Concerns are written in the shift report and told to the on-site manager.

When a resident-to-resident incident occurs, the staff member on duty acts at once: (1) separates the residents and makes sure everyone is safe; (2) assesses each resident for injury and calls EMS if needed; (3) calms the residents and stays with them; (4) tells the on-site manager or administrator immediately.

The administrator or on-site manager then starts the investigation under PCH-08, notifies both residents' representatives or legal surrogates and physicians as needed, and makes the reports that law and rule require. Any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported as set out in PCH-08.

Within 24 hours the administrator or on-site manager revises the care plans of the residents involved. Steps may include a room change, closer supervision, a physician review of behavior, and an assessment of whether the home can still meet each resident's needs (ADM-01 and ADM-03).

The incident, the response, the notices and the care plan changes are recorded in each resident's record and in the central QA file (PCH-11). The QA team looks at the pattern of such incidents each quarter.

If a visitor, proxy caregiver or outside individual is suspected of harming a resident, staff keep the resident safe, tell the administrator at once, preserve evidence, and call 911 where there is an immediate threat. The administrator then reports under PCH-08 and may bar the person.
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and at least annually (PCH-03). The administrator reviews door controls, the visitor log and badge practice at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Completes or oversees applicant screening, sets added safety measures, approves outside individuals, may bar visitors, investigates incidents and makes required reports.
Screens routine outside individuals, enforces visitor sign-in and badge use, and responds to incidents when the administrator is away.
Greet and log visitors, supervise common areas, separate residents in an incident, and report concerns immediately.
Approves the policy and reviews QA reports on resident-to-resident incidents.
Are asked to tell staff about concerns for safety and are told how to report them.

documentation: Admission evaluation with National Sex Offender Registry inquiry or fingerprint check result, date and name of reviewer
Added safety measures recorded in the care plan and admission file
Visitor and vendor sign-in log
Screening records for hospice, home health and other routine outside individuals
Staff, volunteer and proxy caregiver badge records
Incident reports and resident records for resident-to-resident incidents
Revised care plans after incidents
Quarterly QA review notes

policies.category: PCH: Rule 111-8-62-.07(3), policies and procedures (a) through (p)
policies.title: Staffing Plan Based on Resident Needs and Coverage for Absences
policies.applies_to: PCH
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has enough qualified awake staff on duty at all times for the residents it serves, to base staffing on resident needs and to provide backup when scheduled staff are absent.
policies.policy: This policy meets Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07(3)(p) (PCH .07(3)(p)): The staffing plan which takes into account the specific needs of the residents and also includes arrangements for staffing in the absence of regularly scheduled staff. The home keeps a written staffing plan. The plan sets a minimum of one awake direct care staff person for every 15 residents during waking hours and for every 25 residents during non-waking hours. This ratio is the planning minimum used by the home. Note: it comes from third-party-hosted rule text that has not been confirmed against the current official text of Chapter 111-8-62. The administrator will verify the ratio with DCH before the manual is finalized and whenever DCH issues a rule change, and will adopt any stricter requirement at once. The home staffs above this minimum whenever resident needs require it. The plan names backup and on-call staff for any absence. An owner or administrator who lives on the premises or is off duty is not counted as the awake overnight staff person.

definitions.definition: A staff member who is on duty, awake, on the premises and responsible for resident care. The person is not asleep and is not counted while performing duties that take them away from residents for long periods, such as an off-premises errand.

Waking hours are when most residents are normally awake and active. Non-waking hours are the overnight period when most residents are asleep. The home sets the hours in the staffing plan, for example waking hours [START TIME] to [END TIME].
Qualified, oriented and cleared staff who can be called in to cover an absence.
Staff who are scheduled to be reachable and able to arrive within a set time, [NUMBER] minutes, to cover a callout.

procedures: The administrator prepares a written staffing plan before the home admits its first resident. The plan is revised whenever the census or residents' needs change. The plan covers every shift on every day of the week.

The plan states the licensed capacity, the current census, the waking and non-waking hours, the minimum number of awake direct care staff per shift using the 1:15 waking and 1:25 non-waking planning ratio, and the staff scheduled above that minimum.

When the administrator sets the plan, he or she reviews each resident's assessment and care plan (ADM-02). The review looks at mobility and transfer needs, ability to evacuate with or without help, incontinence, dementia and wandering risk, behavior needs, medication needs, number of residents who need two-person assistance, night-time needs and any hospice or home health services. More staff are added when needs require, even if the minimum ratio is met.

The administrator confirms the plan against the building layout. At least one awake staff member must be able to reach and supervise every part of the home where residents are, including each occupied floor and any memory care area (HLT-02).

Every staff member counted in the plan meets the qualifications in PCH-03 and STF-01 before working alone. Managers and responsible staff persons are 21 or older. Staff under 18 may work only under line-of-sight supervision of a qualified adult and are not counted toward the required ratio. New staff complete work-related training, including emergency first aid and CPR certification, within 60 days of hire (PCH-03). Where only one staff member is on duty, that person holds current first aid and CPR certification.

The administrator must meet the qualification rules for the administrator position under Rule 111-8-62-.08, as described in GOV-02. For a home with fewer than 25 beds, that means age 21 or older, and an associate's degree or a GED or high school diploma plus 2 years of licensed PCH or healthcare experience. An administrator who is not on duty and not awake and on site is not counted in the staffing plan.
The administrator posts a written schedule at least [NUMBER] days ahead that shows each shift, the staff name and the backup contact. The schedule is kept on file along with the actual hours worked.

The plan names the people who will cover for absences: at least [NUMBER] trained backup staff and an on-call list with phone numbers and expected arrival times, each of whom has completed orientation, background checks and training. The list is kept in the staff office and updated at least quarterly.

Staff who cannot work a shift must tell the administrator or on-site manager as early as possible and at least [NUMBER] hours before the shift, except in an emergency. The person receiving the call immediately begins calling backup staff in the order on the list and records each call.

If no backup person can arrive on time, the staff member on duty stays until relief comes, if safe and lawful, and the administrator or on-site manager comes in or arranges coverage by a qualified person. The home does not leave residents without the required awake staff. Where coverage cannot be provided, the administrator takes steps to protect residents, which may include calling an agency or alternate caregiver, and records the event.

If staffing falls below the plan, the person in charge records the time, the reason, who was called and how long the shortage lasted, and gives the report to the administrator the same day. The administrator reviews each shortage in the QA process (PCH-11).

The administrator reviews the plan at least monthly, when a resident is admitted, discharged or has a change of condition, after any incident that suggests staffing was a factor, and after any DCH inspection. Each review is dated and signed.

The administrator confirms the ratio and any other staffing standards with DCH ([PHONE]; pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov) before the manual is finalized, records the date and answer, and updates this policy. The administrator repeats the check at least annually.
The administrator keeps the current staffing plan, past plans, schedules, time records and the on-call list on file and available to DCH inspectors at any time, because inspections are unannounced.

responsibilities.duty: Writes and reviews the staffing plan, sets the schedule, keeps the backup and on-call list, verifies ratios with DCH and reviews staffing shortages.
Makes sure each shift meets the plan, takes callout calls, activates backup staff and reports shortages.
Report for scheduled shifts, give early notice of absences, stay until relieved, and remain awake and on duty.
Keep their training and clearances current, answer calls and arrive within the stated time.
Approves the staffing plan and makes sure the home has the budget and people to follow it.

documentation: Written staffing plan with the planning ratio, hours and revision dates
Monthly staffing plan review sign-off
Posted schedules and actual time records
Backup and on-call staff list, with callout and call-back logs
Staffing shortage reports
Record of the DCH ratio verification (date, person spoken to, answer)
Staff qualification, age, CPR and first aid records (see STF-02 and PCH-03)

policies.category: Governance, Licensure and Inspections
policies.title: Licensure, Permit Posting, Licensed Capacity, Inspections and Change of Ownership
policies.applies_to: PCH and ALC
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] holds and keeps a valid DCH permit, never exceeds licensed capacity, markets itself accurately, is ready for unannounced inspections, handles inspection findings on time and follows the required steps if ownership changes.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit any resident until a valid permit has been issued by the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH), Healthcare Facility Regulation Division. The permit is displayed conspicuously where residents and visitors can see it. It is not transferable. It is a separate permit for each premises. The home never has more residents than the licensed capacity shown on the face of the permit (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.06 for assisted living communities; 111-8-62-.06 for personal care homes). The home keeps the permit, annual licence fee, inspection reports and plans of correction current as required by Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.10. Services and marketing must match the permit, the licensed residential care profile and the rules. Only a licensed assisted living community may hold itself out as offering assisted living care, and no home operates a memory care center without a current certificate.

definitions.definition: The licence issued by DCH that allows the home to operate at a specific address with a stated licensed capacity.
The maximum number of residents the permit allows, shown on its face.
A written plan, with date-certain actions, that the home sends to DCH after an inspection reports deficiencies.
A transfer of the home to a new owner or operating entity that requires notice to DCH and residents and a new permit.
The profile the home keeps accurate with DCH, describing its services and the residents it serves.

procedures: Before opening, the administrator confirms that DCH has issued the permit and that the permit shows the correct name, address, classification (PCH or ALC) and licensed capacity. The home does not admit, tour for placement of or accept a deposit for a resident to move in before the permit is issued.
Within one business day of receipt, the administrator posts the permit in a conspicuous place that residents and visitors pass, normally the main lobby. A copy is kept in the administrator's office.

The administrator keeps a daily census. The person in charge checks it against licensed capacity before every admission. No admission is accepted that would exceed the number on the permit. The administrator reviews the census with the governing body at least monthly.

All websites, brochures, advertising and tours must describe the home accurately. An ALC states its licensure classification in marketing. A PCH does not say or imply that it provides assisted living care. A home without a current memory care certificate does not advertise a memory care center or use that term. The administrator approves all marketing in writing before use.

The administrator keeps the licensed residential care profile accurate and makes sure the services described to residents, in the admission agreement and in marketing, match the licence, the profile and the rules.

The administrator keeps a licensure calendar for: the annual licence fee ($350 for a PCH of 2 to 24 beds; $750 for an ALC of 25 to 50 beds; $1,500 for an ALC of 51 or more beds); the memory care certificate fee of $200 per year if the home has one; and renewal dates for the administrator's Board licence where it applies (see GOV-02). The administrator pays at least 30 days before each due date. A $150 late fee applies when payment is 60 days past due, and a replacement permit costs $50. The initial application fee is $300 and is not refundable.

For a new ALC application, the administrator assembles the documents the DCH ALC checklist requires. They include the DCH Office of Health Planning Letter of Determination, a State Fire Marshal report with no violations and the capacity load dated within 12 months, an electrician compliance form dated within 6 months, a private water test dated within 6 months if there is no city or county water, GCHEXS fingerprint checks for administrators and owners of 10% or more (letter within 12 months), and the Affidavit of Compliance. The administrator keeps copies in the licensure file.

The home is subject to unannounced inspections. The administrator keeps all policies, including this manual, in an accessible location and shows them to DCH inspectors on request. Records are available to DCH inspectors at any time. Staff are told in orientation to be courteous, to take the inspector to the administrator or on-site manager right away, and not to refuse access.

When an inspection report is received, the administrator logs the date of receipt the same day. If the home disputes a finding, the written dispute goes to DCH within 10 days of receipt. The written plan of correction, with date-certain actions and a responsible person for each, goes to DCH within 10 days of receipt. The governing body reviews both before they are sent.
The administrator completes each corrective action by the date in the plan and keeps proof. The QA team reviews progress (PCH-11 or ALC-12).

The administrator displays the most recent inspection report and plan of correction where residents and visitors can see them. If the home has a website, it carries a link to the previous 18 months of inspection reports and plans of correction, and the administrator updates it within 10 days of receiving each new report.

If the home plans to move to a new location, the administrator contacts DCH before any move. A permit is no longer valid and must be returned if the home moves to an unlicensed location. A new premises needs its own permit before residents are admitted there.

If the owner plans a change of ownership, the owner gives written notice to DCH and to every resident at least 30 days before the change, or 60 days where bankruptcy or eviction is impending. The notice goes to the resident's representative as well. The existing permit is not transferred. The permit becomes invalid on a change of ownership, and the old permit is returned to DCH. The new owner applies for and obtains a new permit before operating. The administrator keeps proof of delivery of all notices.

If a permit is suspended or revoked, the permit is no longer valid and must be returned. The administrator immediately tells the governing body and obtains legal advice. Residents and representatives are told promptly, and the home works with DCH and others on safe relocation under ADM-03.

No other business is allowed to operate on the premises in a way that interferes with residents' quiet enjoyment of their home. The administrator reviews any proposed business activity on the premises before it begins.

responsibilities.duty: Holds the permit, pays fees, approves plans of correction, gives ownership change notices and stops any activity that threatens the permit.
Posts the permit and inspection reports, tracks capacity and fee dates, approves marketing, hosts inspectors and files disputes and plans of correction within 10 days.
Checks census against licensed capacity before admissions and cooperates with unannounced inspections.
Use only approved, accurate descriptions and do not promise services the licence does not allow.

documentation: Current permit and licensure file, including application documents and DCH correspondence
Daily census and capacity checks
Approved marketing materials and website pages
Licensure fee and renewal calendar, with payment receipts
Inspection reports, written disputes, plans of correction and proof of timely submission
Proof of posting of the permit and the latest report, and the website link log
Change of ownership notices to DCH and residents, with delivery proof
Memory care certificate, where applicable

policies.category: Governance, Licensure and Inspections
policies.title: Governing Body, Administrator Qualifications, DCH Contact Information and Document Control
policies.applies_to: PCH and ALC
policies.purpose: To establish the governing body that oversees [AGENCY NAME], to make sure the administrator meets Georgia qualifications, to keep DCH informed of current contacts and to control the policy manual so that the current approved version is always in use.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has a functioning governing body. It oversees compliance with the applicable rules: for a personal care home, Title 31 Chapter 7 and DCH Chapters 111-8-25, 111-8-62 and 111-8-100 (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.07); for an assisted living community, Chapters 111-8-63, 111-8-25 and 111-8-100 (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.07). The governing body implements policies that support dignity, respect, choice, independence and privacy for residents. The governing body keeps DCH supplied with current contact information and holds staff accountable for delivering DCH notices to it. The home employs an administrator who meets the qualification rules for its size. The governing body reviews and approves this manual at least annually.

definitions.definition: The owner, board or other group with legal authority over the home and responsibility for its operation, policies and compliance.
The person responsible for the day-to-day operation of the home who meets the qualifications for the home's size.
A responsible person designated to manage the home when the administrator is not present.
The system that keeps one approved current version of each policy, a revision log and a record of who approved each change.

procedures: The owner names the members of the governing body in writing, with their roles and contact information, and records this in the governing body minutes. The body meets at least quarterly and keeps minutes.

The governing body discloses to DCH, in the initial application, all owners with 10% or more and the registered agent. The administrator updates this disclosure with DCH whenever it changes. The application states the name of the administrator or on-site manager before the permit is issued (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.05).

For an initial application for a home of 25 or more beds, the governing body obtains a CPA financial stability affidavit (going concern for 2 years) and submits it with the application. The governing body also addresses local zoning with the responsible local officials before applying.

The governing body makes sure the administrator meets Rule 111-8-62-.08 or the applicable ALC rule before the person starts work. For a PCH with fewer than 25 beds the administrator must be 21 or older and hold an associate's degree, or a GED or high school diploma plus 2 years of licensed PCH or healthcare experience. The administrator's qualifications are checked against documents and kept in the personnel file.

For a home of 25 or more beds (an ALC or a PCH of that size), the administrator must hold a valid licence from the Georgia State Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators within 60 days of hire. The governing body confirms the application is filed in that time. The Board's phone is 404-424-9966. The initial application requires at least one year of full-time experience (1,560 hours in the preceding 12 months) and a board-approved administration program. The Board charges a $100 application fee plus a $10 paper or $5 online processing fee. The administrator confirms the current fee with the Board before filing. The licence is biennial and expires on December 31 of odd-numbered years. The administrator keeps the licence renewal date on the licensure calendar (GOV-01) and renews before it expires.

The administrator designates in writing an on-site manager for any time the administrator is not present, and the designee must meet the age and training requirements in PCH-03, PCH-14 or ALC-04. The designee's name is given to DCH as required.

The administrator keeps DCH supplied with current contact information: the name, email address for notices, physical address and phone numbers of the governing body and of the administrator or on-site manager. DCH's personal care home program contact is pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov. The administrator sends written updates to DCH within [NUMBER] business days of any change and keeps a copy of each update and any acknowledgment.

All staff are told to hand any DCH notice, letter, email or inspection report to the administrator or on-site manager immediately. The administrator logs the date of receipt and sends a copy to the governing body within one business day. Staff who do not deliver a DCH notice are subject to discipline under PCH-09 or ALC-10.

The governing body adopts the policies that Georgia rules require (see the PCH-01 to PCH-14 or ALC-01 to ALC-14 series), and makes sure they support dignity, respect, choice, independence and privacy. The body oversees the home's compliance through the administrator's reports, QA summaries (PCH-11 or ALC-12), inspection reports and resident feedback.

The administrator keeps the manual in a master binder or electronic file in an easy-to-reach location so that it is available to DCH inspectors at any time. Each policy shows an identification number, title, effective date, version number and approval date. Staff can read the manual at all times.

Policy changes are drafted by the administrator, reviewed by the governing body and approved by a dated signature. The administrator then adds the change to the revision log with the date, the policy changed, the reason and the approver. Replaced versions are marked superseded and kept for [NUMBER] years in an archive.
After each approved change the administrator trains affected staff within [NUMBER] days, collects signed acknowledgments and removes old copies from use.

The governing body reviews the whole manual at least annually, and sooner when DCH changes a rule, after an inspection finding, a serious incident or a QA recommendation. The review is recorded in the minutes and the revision log, and the manual is signed and dated again.

The administrator checks DCH's website and rule text at least twice a year for updates. Items in this manual that are marked for verification, such as staffing ratios, are confirmed with DCH and the answer is recorded in the document control file.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees compliance, adopts and annually approves the manual, hires a qualified administrator, discloses ownership and keeps DCH contact details current.
Meets and maintains qualifications and the Board licence where required, keeps the manual and revision log, updates DCH contacts, logs DCH notices and trains staff on changes.
Is designated in writing, meets qualifications and receives DCH notices when the administrator is absent.
Know where the manual is, follow it, and hand DCH notices to the administrator at once.

documentation: Governing body roster, minutes and annual manual approval signature page
Ownership disclosure (owners with 10% or more and registered agent) and CPA financial stability affidavit for initial 25-or-more-bed applications
Administrator qualification file: education, experience, age proof and, where required, Board of Long-Term Care Facility Administrators licence and renewal dates
Written designation of the on-site manager
DCH contact information updates and DCH notice log
Master policy manual, revision log, dated approval signatures and superseded-policy archive
Staff acknowledgments of policy changes
Record of DCH verification on items marked for confirmation

policies.category: Resident Rights
policies.title: Grievances, Complaints and Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (ch. 111-8-63) operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give every resident, representative and family member a simple, safe and respected way to raise a concern, to make sure each concern is investigated and answered, and to keep residents in direct contact with the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program and the Georgia Department of Community Health (DCH).
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] welcomes complaints and treats them as information that helps us improve care. The admission agreement describes the complaint process (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.16). Residents have access to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program (O.C.G.A. 31-8-50 et seq.), and the name, address and phone number of the assigned ombudsman are posted in a common area (111-8-63-.25(v)). No resident, representative or staff member will be punished, harassed, threatened or treated differently for making a complaint or for enforcing a resident's rights (111-8-63-.25). Residents are told that they may complain to DCH at any time, with or without first using the community's process. Every grievance is logged, investigated, answered and documented through resolution. Rights under this policy cannot be waived by the community or by staff. This policy is adopted for personal care homes to implement the corresponding resident-rights and complaint requirements of ch. 111-8-62.

definitions.definition: Any oral, written or electronic expression of dissatisfaction or concern by a resident, representative, legal surrogate, family member or staff member about care, services, staff conduct, other residents, the physical environment, fees or the exercise of rights.
A representative of the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program (O.C.G.A. 31-8-50 et seq.) who advocates for residents and may receive and help resolve complaints.
Any punishment, harassment, discrimination, threat of discharge, reduction in service or other adverse treatment because someone made a complaint or enforced a right.
The administrator, or a staff member designated in writing by the administrator, who receives and manages grievances.

procedures: At or before admission, the administrator or designee reviews the complaint process in the admission agreement with the resident and representative, explains it in plain language and records that this was done in the resident file.

At admission, staff give the resident and representative the name and contact information of the Grievance Officer, the assigned ombudsman's name, address and phone number, and DCH's contact information for complaints (email: pchprogram.hfrd@dch.ga.gov; phone: [DCH COMPLAINT PHONE]).

The administrator posts the assigned ombudsman's name, address and phone number in a common area where residents can see it, with the DCH complaint contact next to it. The administrator checks monthly that the posting is current and legible and initials the posting log.

Any staff member who receives a complaint, whether oral or written, listens respectfully, writes down what was said on the Grievance Form the same shift, and gives it to the Grievance Officer. Staff never discourage a complaint or ask the resident to withdraw it.

If the complaint involves suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation, injury or an immediate risk to health or safety, staff notify the administrator immediately and follow the community's abuse, neglect and incident-reporting policy ([ALC-09] / [PCH-08]) in addition to this policy.

The Grievance Officer enters the grievance in the Grievance Log within one business day, recording: date received, name of the complainant, resident affected, nature of the concern, and who received it.
The Grievance Officer acknowledges the complaint to the complainant, orally or in writing, within two business days. This is the community's internal standard.

The Grievance Officer starts an investigation promptly. This includes interviewing the complainant, the resident, witnesses and involved staff, and reviewing the record, schedules and any other relevant information. Anyone alleged to have committed misconduct is not involved in investigating the complaint.

The Grievance Officer gives the complainant a written or oral response, as the complainant prefers, within [GRIEVANCE RESPONSE DAYS, not to exceed 14] calendar days of receipt. The response states what was found, what action was taken and how to appeal or contact the ombudsman or DCH if the complainant is not satisfied.

If a complainant is dissatisfied, the administrator personally reviews the grievance and meets with the complainant, with the ombudsman present if the complainant asks. The outcome is recorded in the log.
The Grievance Log records, for each grievance: the investigation steps, the response date, the resolution, any corrective action and the date the complainant was told of the result.
The administrator reviews the Grievance Log at least monthly to spot patterns and gives a summary to the governing body and the Quality Assurance review ([ALC-12] / [PCH-11]) each quarter.

Staff are trained at hire and annually that retaliation is prohibited. Any report of retaliation is investigated by the administrator, and confirmed retaliation is handled under the staff discipline policy ([ALC-10] / [PCH-09]).
The administrator allows the ombudsman reasonable access to residents, including private visits, and does not screen or restrict communication between a resident and the ombudsman.

The administrator tells residents at least annually, such as at a resident council or meeting, how to file a complaint and that they may also complain to DCH or the ombudsman. The date and attendance are recorded.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the grievance process, serves as or designates the Grievance Officer, posts and maintains ombudsman and DCH information, reviews the log monthly, and prevents retaliation.
Logs, acknowledges, investigates and answers each grievance on time and documents the resolution.
Receive any complaint respectfully, document it the same shift, pass it to the Grievance Officer, and never retaliate or discourage complaints.
Reviews quarterly grievance summaries and ensures that the process is working and that corrective action is taken.

documentation: Grievance Forms
Grievance Log with investigation notes, response dates and resolutions
Written responses to complainants, where made in writing
Record of admission-time review of the complaint process in the resident file
Ombudsman and DCH posting log
Quarterly grievance summaries to the governing body and the QA file

policies.category: Resident Rights
policies.title: Admission Agreement, Fees, Rate Increases and Deposits
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (ch. 111-8-63) operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident and representative receives a clear, plain-language admission agreement that states all charges and what they cover, receives required advance notice of rate increases, and knows how deposits and refunds are handled.
policies.policy: Every resident is admitted under a written, plain-language admission agreement that is consistent with the community's licensed residential care profile (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.16). The agreement states all fees and what each fee covers. [AGENCY NAME] gives written notice at least 30 days before any increase in personal-service charges and at least 60 days before any increase in room-and-board charges. The agreement includes provisions for continuous assessment and for referral or transfer on a change of condition, a description of the complaint process, transportation terms (with emergency transport available at all times), and a refund policy that applies on death, transfer or discharge. The governing body adopts the form of agreement and approves the refund policy as part of its oversight of admissions, discharges and refunds (111-8-63-.07). A Georgia attorney reviews the agreement before it is first used and when it is materially changed. The agreement is signed by the resident or the representative or legal surrogate and kept in the resident file. This policy is adopted for personal care homes to implement the corresponding requirements of ch. 111-8-62.

definitions.definition: The written contract between the community and the resident (or representative) setting out services, fees, responsibilities, transportation, complaint process, refund terms and conditions for transfer or discharge.
Fees for personal services and care provided to a resident, as itemized in the agreement, excluding room and board.
Fees for lodging, meals and the basic housing services described in the agreement.
Any money paid before or at admission that is held as a security deposit, reservation or other advance payment, as described in the agreement.
A person authorized by the resident or by law to act for the resident. No member of the governing body, administration or staff, or their family, may serve as a legal surrogate (see RR-04).

procedures: The governing body adopts a standard admission agreement written in plain language, at a reading level a typical resident can follow, and consistent with the community's licensed residential care profile.

Before first use, and again after any material change to the agreement or fee schedule, a Georgia attorney retained by [AGENCY NAME] reviews the agreement. The administrator keeps the attorney's review date in the document-control file.

The agreement lists every fee, including base rate, room-and-board charges, personal-service or care-level charges, and each separately charged item such as medication management or incontinence supplies, and states what each fee covers. There are no unlisted fees.

The agreement includes provisions for continuous assessment and for referral or transfer when the resident's condition changes, consistent with the Resident Assessment policy (ADM-02) and Discharge and Transfer policy (ADM-03).
The agreement describes the complaint process, including how to reach the Grievance Officer, the ombudsman and DCH (see RR-01).
The agreement states transportation terms, including which transportation is provided, which is charged and at what rate, and that emergency transport is available at all times.

The agreement states the refund policy that applies on death, transfer or discharge: how unused fees and any deposit are calculated, what may be deducted, and the time within which the refund is paid. The refund terms are the same as those approved by the governing body.

Before signing, the administrator or designee meets with the resident and representative, reads or explains the agreement in plain language (using an interpreter or other aids as needed, see RR-06), answers questions and allows time to review. The resident and representative are given a copy.

The resident, or the representative or legal surrogate if the resident cannot, signs and dates the agreement. The administrator or designee also signs. No one is asked to sign blank pages or a document that has not been explained.
The signed agreement is placed in the resident file the day it is signed and the resident file checklist is initialed.

For a deposit, staff give a dated receipt stating the amount, purpose and conditions of return. The deposit is recorded in the resident's financial ledger and kept separate from operating funds as described in the agreement. The community does not require payment beyond what the agreement states.

To raise any personal-service charge, the administrator sends written notice to the resident and representative at least 30 days before the effective date, stating the old charge, the new charge and the effective date. A copy is kept in the resident file with a record of how and when it was delivered.

To raise any room-and-board charge, the administrator sends written notice at least 60 days before the effective date, with the same content. A change in the services a resident receives that is driven by an assessed change of condition, and the charge that follows, is documented in an updated service plan and signed addendum.

On a death, transfer or discharge, the administrator calculates the refund according to the agreement, prepares an itemized statement and issues the refund and statement within the time stated in the agreement. A copy is kept in the file.

The administrator reviews the agreement template at least annually with the governing body and whenever a rule changes. Residents are given any revised agreement as an addendum with the required notice.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the admission agreement and the refund policy, approves fee schedules and rate increases, and ensures attorney review.
Explains and executes agreements, issues required rate-increase notices on time, handles deposits and refunds, and keeps the signed agreement in the file.
Maintains financial ledgers, prepares refund calculations and keeps records of notices.
Reviews the agreement template and material revisions for legal sufficiency.

documentation: Signed admission agreement in the resident file
Attorney review record in the document-control file
Current fee schedule approved by the governing body
Dated 30-day and 60-day rate-increase notices with delivery records
Deposit receipts and ledger entries
Itemized refund statements and refund records
Record of agreement review meeting with the resident and representative

policies.category: Resident Rights
policies.title: Resident Funds, Valuables and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (ch. 111-8-63) operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect residents' money, valuables and belongings from loss, misuse and exploitation by keeping accurate records, keeping resident funds separate from the community's, and never pressuring any resident to give property to the community.
policies.policy: Residents own and control their money, valuables and personal property. [AGENCY NAME] will not manage a resident's funds or hold valuables unless the resident or representative asks in writing. When we do, we keep a record of monetary transactions with itemized receipts and give a receipt for any valuables held in safekeeping, and we keep an inventory of personal valuables in the resident file (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.24). No resident will be coerced to assign money, valuables or property to the community (111-8-63-.25). Resident funds are kept separate from operating funds. The administrator signs a reconciliation of all resident funds held every quarter. This policy is adopted for personal care homes to implement the corresponding requirements of ch. 111-8-62.

definitions.definition: Money belonging to a resident that the community holds or manages at the resident's or representative's written request, including personal-needs funds.
Items of significant monetary or sentimental value, such as jewelry, cash, documents or checkbooks, that the community stores for a resident at the resident's request.
A dated, signed list of the resident's valuable belongings brought to the community, kept in the resident file.
Improper use of a resident's funds, property or resources by another person for profit or advantage, as defined in the applicable chapter's definitions.

procedures: At admission, the administrator or designee explains to the resident and representative that the resident may keep and manage money and valuables personally, may ask the community to hold them, or may use a family member or other representative. The choice is recorded in the resident file.

Staff and the resident (or representative) complete and sign a Personal Valuables Inventory at admission, listing items such as jewelry, electronics and significant furnishings, with a description of each. A copy goes to the resident and the original goes in the resident file.

Staff update the inventory whenever the resident or family brings in or removes an item of value, and the resident or representative signs the update. The inventory is reviewed with the resident at least annually.
The community holds funds or valuables only on the resident's or representative's written request. The request states what is to be held and may be withdrawn at any time.

For each valuable held, two staff members count and describe the item with the resident or representative, and a written, dated, signed receipt is given to the resident. A copy is placed in the resident file. Valuables are kept in a locked location that only the administrator and one designated person can open.

For each deposit or withdrawal of resident funds, staff record the date, amount, purpose and running balance in the individual resident ledger and give the resident an itemized receipt. The resident or representative signs for any withdrawal.
Resident funds are kept in a separate account or separate locked fund from operating funds. Resident money is never used to pay community expenses, mixed with petty cash or used as a loan.

Staff may not borrow from or lend money to residents, accept gifts of value, serve as a resident's agent for money, be named in a resident's will or be added to a resident's account, except as the administrator approves in writing under the code of conduct.

No staff member, volunteer or owner will ask, pressure or suggest that any resident sign over money, valuables, property, bank accounts or powers of attorney to the community or to any individual connected with it. Any such attempt is reported to the administrator immediately and treated as suspected exploitation under [ALC-09] / [PCH-08].

Every quarter, the business office reconciles each resident ledger to the account or cash held and to receipts. The administrator reviews and signs and dates the reconciliation, noting and resolving any discrepancy within five business days.

If a resident reports missing property, staff complete an incident report the same shift, search with the resident's permission, notify the representative, and the administrator investigates. Findings and the response are recorded and the resident is told the result (see RR-01).

At discharge, transfer or death, staff return all funds and valuables with an itemized final accounting. The resident, representative or the person lawfully entitled to the property signs a receipt. After a death, property is released only to the legal representative of the estate or as law directs, and the administrator documents it.
Annually, the administrator reviews a sample of resident ledgers and valuables receipts and reports the results to the governing body and the Quality Assurance review ([ALC-12] / [PCH-11]).

responsibilities.duty: Controls access to funds and valuables, signs quarterly reconciliations, investigates losses and ensures no coercion occurs.
Keeps ledgers and itemized receipts, deposits and withdrawals, and prepares reconciliations.
Assist with inventories, never handle resident funds unless authorized, and report missing items or suspected exploitation immediately.
Receives annual review results and ensures separation of resident and operating funds.

documentation: Personal Valuables Inventory and updates
Written request to hold funds or valuables
Resident financial ledgers with itemized receipts
Safekeeping receipts for valuables
Signed quarterly reconciliation
Missing-property incident reports and investigation results
Final accounting and release receipts at discharge or death

policies.category: Resident Rights
policies.title: Advance Directives, Legal Surrogates and Powers of Attorney
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (ch. 111-8-63) operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents' end-of-life wishes and decision-makers are known, recorded and honored, that staff can find a resident's code status quickly in an emergency, and that no one with a conflict of interest serves as a resident's legal surrogate.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects each resident's right to make or refuse medical decisions. Forms for a living will, a durable power of attorney for health care (DPOA-HC) and a Georgia advance directive are available to residents at admission. Any living will, DPOA-HC, Georgia advance directive and signed end-of-life medical orders are kept in the resident file (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.24). A copy of any power of attorney is also kept in the file (111-8-62-.03). No member of the governing body, administration or staff, or any of their family members, may serve as a resident's legal surrogate (111-8-62-.03). In an emergency, staff follow the resident's directives as set out in 111-8-63-.26: a valid DNR is honored in good faith; if there is a health care agent, staff call the agent; otherwise staff call EMS and start CPR. The community does not give legal advice and does not require a resident to have or not have an advance directive as a condition of admission. This policy is adopted for personal care homes to implement the corresponding requirements of ch. 111-8-62.

definitions.definition: A written document in which a resident states wishes about future medical treatment, including a Georgia advance directive for health care.
A durable power of attorney for health care naming a person (the health care agent) to make health care decisions for the resident, governed by O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq.
A physician-signed order, or other signed end-of-life medical order, stating that CPR is not to be started, or setting out other limits on treatment.
A person with legal authority to act for the resident. No member of the governing body, administration or staff, or their family members, may serve in this role.
A written document by which a resident authorizes another person to act on the resident's behalf, for example in financial matters.

procedures: At admission, the administrator or designee asks every resident or representative whether the resident has a living will, DPOA-HC, Georgia advance directive, DNR or other end-of-life medical orders, or a power of attorney, and records the answer on the Admission Checklist.

Staff make blank advance directive and DPOA-HC forms available to every resident at admission and explain that completing them is the resident's choice. Staff do not complete the forms for the resident, witness or sign as agent, or influence the resident's choices.

If the resident has any of these documents, staff obtain a copy, place it in the resident file in the section marked 'Advance Directives' and record the date received. Original documents stay with the resident or representative unless the resident asks otherwise.

Staff place a copy of any power of attorney in the resident file and note on the face sheet who holds it and the type of authority granted. Staff do not accept the document as proof of authority if it looks incomplete or altered; the administrator reviews and, if necessary, asks for clarification from the resident or the resident's attorney.

Before accepting any person as a legal surrogate or representative, the administrator checks that the person is not a member of the governing body, administration or staff, and is not a family member of any of them. If this conflict exists, the community does not recognize the person as legal surrogate and tells the resident and family in writing that another surrogate is needed.

The administrator records the resident's code status (full code, DNR, hospice) and health care agent contact information on a face sheet at the front of the resident file and on the emergency information sheet that goes with the resident to the hospital.

All staff are trained at hire and annually on where to find code status and agent contact information within one minute, on the emergency procedure below, and on the need to keep resident information ready during transport.
If a resident is found unresponsive and is a hospice enrollee, staff call the hospice first, then the health care agent, then EMS and start CPR if there is no DNR.

If a resident is found unresponsive and has a valid DNR, staff honor it in good faith. Staff stay with the resident, notify the physician, hospice if enrolled, the representative and the administrator, and document the event.
If the resident has a health care agent under O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq., staff call the agent. If the agent cannot be reached and there is no DNR, staff call EMS and start CPR.

If there is no hospice, DNR or directive, staff call EMS and start CPR, except where the rule allows otherwise because the resident's condition is clearly futile and no physician, authorized registered nurse or physician assistant is on site. Staff do not make a futility judgment on their own; they follow the instructions of the 911 dispatcher and the administrator.

Staff send the face sheet, code status, medication list and agent contact information with the resident to the hospital and ensure staff have ready access to emergency numbers and resident information during transport.

After any emergency, the administrator or on-site manager records the event and the response in the resident file and follows the change-of-condition policy (HLT-01) and incident policy ([ALC-09] / [PCH-08]).
When a resident's wishes change or a new document is signed, staff replace the earlier copy, mark the old copy superseded and update the face sheet and emergency sheet the same day.
The administrator reviews each resident's advance directive status at every reassessment and at least annually, and offers the resident the chance to review or update the documents.
The administrator audits all resident files quarterly to confirm that directives, orders, power of attorney copies and the surrogate conflict check are present and consistent with the face sheet.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures forms are available, directives are filed, the surrogate conflict check is done and staff are trained in the emergency procedure.
Ask about directives and POAs at admission, obtain copies, update the face sheet and the emergency sheet.
Know where to find code status, follow the emergency steps in 111-8-63-.26 and keep resident information available during transport.
Provide documents, keep them current and tell staff of any change.

documentation: Living will, DPOA-HC, Georgia advance directive and signed end-of-life medical orders in the resident file
Copies of powers of attorney
Face sheet and emergency information sheet showing code status and health care agent
Surrogate conflict-of-interest check
Admission checklist entry for advance directives
Emergency event documentation
Quarterly file audit results

policies.category: Resident Rights
policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (ch. 111-8-63) operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the privacy of residents' personal, health and financial information and their personal space, and to meet Georgia confidentiality requirements and, where applicable, the federal HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules.
policies.policy: Each resident file is confidential. It may be disclosed only to the resident, the representative or legal surrogate, agents of DCH, and those with the resident's written authorization (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.24). The resident and representative may inspect and copy the file, and DCH may inspect and copy it. Staff knock before entering a resident's room, and residents have the right to free, private communication without staff censorship (111-8-63-.25). If [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, for example because it bills Medicaid electronically, it will designate a privacy officer, issue a notice of privacy practices and sign business associate agreements, and will follow 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164. Photographs, video, social media posts and marketing uses of a resident's name or image require the resident's or representative's written consent. This policy is adopted for personal care homes to implement the corresponding requirements of ch. 111-8-62.

definitions.definition: The individual file kept for each resident containing identifying, health, financial, legal and admission information.
Individually identifiable health information, in any form, held by the community, to the extent covered by HIPAA (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164).
A health care provider, health plan or clearinghouse that is subject to HIPAA, including a provider that conducts certain standard transactions, such as electronic Medicaid billing, electronically.

A person or company outside the community's workforce that creates, receives, maintains or transmits PHI on the community's behalf, such as a pharmacy services vendor, billing company or software provider.
A signed and dated document by the resident or representative that allows disclosure of identified information to a named person or organization for a stated purpose.

procedures: The administrator determines and records, with the governing body and legal counsel, whether the community is a HIPAA covered entity. This determination is reviewed whenever billing practices change, for example when the community begins billing Medicaid electronically (see MCD-01).

If the community is a covered entity, the administrator designates a privacy officer in writing and posts the officer's name and contact information. Until a different person is designated, the administrator is the privacy officer.

If covered, the community gives each resident or representative a notice of privacy practices at admission, asks for a signed acknowledgment, posts the notice in a common area and keeps the acknowledgment in the file.

Resident files are kept in a locked cabinet or in a password-protected electronic system with access limited by job role. Files are not left open on desks or screens, and are not taken off site except as the administrator authorizes.
Staff access files only to the extent needed to do their jobs. Each staff member signs a confidentiality statement at hire and the statement is placed in the personnel file.

Before disclosing any information from a resident file, staff confirm that the request is from the resident, representative or legal surrogate, an authorized DCH agent, or a person with written authorization from the resident. Staff ask for identification of the person and record the date, requester, information released and staff member who released it.

The resident or representative may ask to inspect or copy the file. Staff arrange a time promptly, no later than [FILE ACCESS DAYS, not to exceed 3] business days, stay with the person during review to keep the file intact and provide copies on request. DCH agents are given access during inspections.

Staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's room, except in an emergency. Personal care is provided with the door closed and the resident covered. Staff do not discuss residents in hallways, dining rooms or other public places.

Mail, telephone calls, email and other communication for residents are delivered unopened and promptly. Staff do not read, censor or withhold a resident's communication. Residents have access to a telephone in a private location.

The administrator obtains written authorization from the resident or representative before taking or using any photograph, video or recording of a resident, or before using a resident's name, image or story on social media, in marketing materials or on the website. Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Staff are prohibited from taking resident photos on personal devices.

Where the community is a covered entity, it signs a business associate agreement with each vendor that handles PHI and keeps the agreements on file. The administrator reviews the list of vendors annually.

Staff report any suspected unauthorized access, loss or disclosure of resident information to the privacy officer immediately. The privacy officer investigates within [BREACH REVIEW DAYS, not to exceed 5] business days, takes corrective steps, makes any notifications required by law with legal counsel and records the outcome.
All staff are trained on privacy and confidentiality at hire and annually. Violations are handled under the staff discipline policy ([ALC-10] / [PCH-09]).
Electronic records are protected by unique user IDs, password controls, automatic log-off and regular backups. Devices holding resident information are locked when unattended.
The administrator reviews privacy practices, including file security, disclosure logs and photo consents, at least annually and reports to the governing body.

responsibilities.duty: Controls access to resident files, determines covered-entity status, trains staff and ensures privacy practices are followed.
Maintains the notice of privacy practices, handles complaints and breach reviews, and manages business associate agreements.
Protect resident information, knock before entering rooms, release information only as permitted, and report any suspected breach.
Oversees privacy compliance and approves policies on resident information.

documentation: Covered-entity determination
Privacy officer designation and notice of privacy practices with signed acknowledgments (if covered)
Staff confidentiality statements
Disclosure log and written authorizations
Records of resident or representative file access and copying
Photograph, video and marketing consent forms
Business associate agreements (if covered)
Breach investigation records and training records

policies.category: Resident Rights
policies.title: Nondiscrimination, Disability Access and Language Access
policies.applies_to: Personal Care Homes (ch. 111-8-62) and Assisted Living Communities (ch. 111-8-63) operated by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure that every applicant and resident is treated fairly and with dignity regardless of race, national origin, religion, sex or disability, that residents with disabilities and residents with limited English proficiency can understand and use our services, and that residents keep choice over their activities and schedules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] makes admission decisions based on the admission profile and its ability to meet the applicant's needs, never on race, national origin, religion, sex or disability. The admission agreement is written in plain language (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.16). We provide interpreters and translated key documents for residents with limited English proficiency, consistent with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. 2000d). We provide reasonable accommodations for residents with disabilities and welcome service animals, as required by the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. 12101 et seq.). Residents choose their own activities and schedules (111-8-63-.25). A nondiscrimination notice is posted in a common area. Language and disability access services are provided at no charge to the resident. This policy is adopted for personal care homes to implement the corresponding requirements of ch. 111-8-62.

definitions.definition: A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English well enough to communicate effectively about health care and services.

A change in a rule, policy, practice or service, or the provision of an aid, that allows a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the services, unless it would fundamentally alter the service or impose an undue burden or direct threat.
A dog (or, in limited cases, a miniature horse) individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, as defined under the ADA.

A person who is competent in both languages and in interpreting, who is impartial and who is not a family member or another resident unless the resident asks for that person after being offered a qualified interpreter.
The description of the residents the community is licensed and able to serve, including its ability to meet care needs, as set out in the licensed residential care profile and admission policies.

procedures: The governing body adopts this policy and the administrator posts a nondiscrimination notice in a common area and on the website. The notice says that the community does not discriminate on the basis of race, national origin, religion, sex or disability and tells people how to file a complaint with the community (RR-01) or an outside agency.

At the first inquiry, staff offer information about our services and admission requirements to everyone in the same way. Admission decisions are made by the administrator using the written admission criteria and the ability to meet the person's assessed needs (ADM-01), not on any protected characteristic.

If an applicant is declined, the administrator writes down the specific, needs-based reason, such as care needs beyond what the community is authorized or able to provide, and keeps the record in the admissions file. The reason is explained to the applicant and representative and, where requested, given in writing.

At first contact and at admission, staff ask the resident or representative what language the resident prefers for communication and for written materials and whether the resident has any communication needs, including hearing, vision, speech or cognitive needs. The answer is recorded on the face sheet.

For a resident with limited English proficiency, staff provide a qualified interpreter, in person or by telephone or video, for the admission process, assessments, consent discussions, care planning, grievances and any important health or safety conversation, at no cost to the resident. Staff do not require or ask the resident to bring a family member to interpret. A family member or friend may interpret only if the resident requests it after being offered a qualified interpreter, and this is documented.

The administrator makes sure that key documents are available in the languages of residents the community serves, including the admission agreement summary, resident rights, grievance procedure, house rules, evacuation instructions and the nondiscrimination notice. Where a translation is not available, the content is interpreted orally and documented.

The admission agreement and other resident materials are written in plain language. Staff read or explain the documents aloud for residents who need that and offer large-print, audio or other formats on request (see RR-02).

When a resident or applicant asks for a reasonable accommodation, such as a ramp, grab bars, a modified schedule, an adapted communication method or help with a form, staff write down the request and give it to the administrator the same day. The administrator decides promptly, usually within [ACCOMMODATION RESPONSE DAYS, not to exceed 5] business days, after talking with the resident. If a request cannot be granted as made, the administrator offers an effective alternative and records the reason.

The community welcomes service animals. Staff may ask only two questions: whether the animal is required because of a disability and what work or task it has been trained to perform. Staff do not ask about the person's disability, require documentation or charge a pet fee or deposit for a service animal. The resident remains responsible for the animal's care and control. The administrator may exclude an animal that is out of control and not corrected or that is not housebroken, and records the reason.

Residents choose their activities and daily schedules, including when to get up, go to bed, eat where options are available and participate in or decline activities (111-8-63-.25). Staff accommodate religious practice and cultural, dietary and personal preferences where possible and record them in the care plan.

Staff are trained at hire and annually on nondiscrimination, respectful treatment, disability etiquette, using interpreters and responding to accommodation and service animal requests. The training is recorded in the personnel file.

Any complaint about discrimination is handled as a grievance under RR-01, investigated by the administrator, and answered in writing. Staff who are found to have discriminated are disciplined under [ALC-10] / [PCH-09]. No one is retaliated against for raising a concern.

The administrator reviews, at least annually, the languages used by residents and applicants, accommodation requests and their outcomes, declined admissions and grievances, and reports to the governing body and the Quality Assurance review ([ALC-12] / [PCH-11]).

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the nondiscrimination policy and ensures resources for interpreters, translation and accommodations.
Posts the notice, decides admission and accommodation requests, arranges interpreters and translations, trains staff and reviews data annually.
Treat everyone equally and respectfully, record language and communication needs, use qualified interpreters and pass accommodation requests to the administrator the same day.
Tell staff about language and communication needs and request accommodations when needed.

documentation: Posted nondiscrimination notice
Documented reasons for any declined admission
Face sheet entry of preferred language and communication needs
Interpreter use records
Translated documents on file
Accommodation request log with decisions and reasons
Service animal records
Training records and annual review report

policies.category: Admission, Retention and Discharge
policies.title: Pre-Admission Screening, Admission Criteria and Retention Limits
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Community (ALC, Ch. 111-8-63). A Personal Care Home (PCH, Ch. 111-8-62) adopts the same screening steps as agency policy to the extent they are consistent with its own permit and rules.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and keeps only residents whose needs it is authorized and able to meet. Screening is documented and consistent. It protects the applicant, current residents and staff, and it keeps the community within its licensed capacity.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits an applicant only after a documented pre-admission evaluation by the administrator or on-site manager shows that the applicant meets the admission profile in Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.15(1). The applicant must be 18 or older and free of active tuberculosis. The applicant must not need continuous medical or nursing care. The applicant must not need physical or chemical restraints, isolation or confinement for behavioral control. The applicant must be able to take an active part in transfers and be able to take part in social and leisure activities. The evaluation includes a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry or a fingerprint check. Where the result calls for it, the evaluation also documents added safety measures for a registered sex offender or violent offender (.15(2)). The admission packet includes a physician examination on the DCH-required form (.15). Admission and retention decisions must not exceed the care the community is authorized or able to provide (.07(2)(c)), and the community's services are those described in .17. [AGENCY NAME] never admits a resident that would exceed licensed capacity. If an applicant does not meet these criteria, or if a current resident no longer meets them, [AGENCY NAME] declines admission or begins the transfer process in ADM-03. The agency documents the reason in either case.

definitions.definition: A person who has asked to move into the community and whose admission has not yet been decided.
The person who holds the administrator role under GOV-02, or the designated manager in charge on site, who makes and documents the admission decision.
Care that must be given around the clock by a nurse or physician. A resident who needs it cannot be admitted or retained.
A physical or chemical restraint as defined in the licensing rules and in SAF-02. Using one for behavioral control makes the person ineligible for admission or retention.
The maximum number of residents shown on the permit. It is never exceeded.

procedures: The administrator or on-site manager handles every inquiry. Staff give prospective residents and families a written description of the services the community provides and does not provide, and the fee schedule from RR-02.

Before any admission decision, the administrator or on-site manager (or a person they designate in writing) completes a pre-admission screening with the applicant and the representative or legal surrogate. The screening is in person or by video and includes review of the applicant's medical, functional, cognitive and behavioral history.

The applicant must supply a physician examination on the DCH-required form. The form must be current, signed and complete, and it must show that the applicant is free of active tuberculosis. If it is incomplete, the administrator returns it to the physician and does not admit until it is complete.

The administrator or on-site manager checks each admission criterion against the file: age 18 or older; no active TB; no need for continuous medical or nursing care; no need for restraints, isolation or confinement; ability to take part in transfers; and ability to take part in social and leisure activities. The result of each check is recorded on the Admission Screening Checklist.

Before the decision, the administrator or on-site manager runs a National Sex Offender Registry inquiry (or obtains a fingerprint check) on the applicant. They print or save the result, date and sign it, and file it in the resident record.

If the applicant is a registered sex offender or has a history of violence, the administrator documents the specific added safety measures to be used. These may include supervision level, room placement, notice to staff on a need-to-know basis, and a review date. The measures are documented before admission. The decision is not made on the registry result alone: it also considers whether the community can keep other residents safe.

The administrator or on-site manager compares the applicant's identified needs with the services [AGENCY NAME] is authorized and staffed to provide, including staffing under ALC-02 and any memory care limits under HLT-02. If the needs exceed what the community can provide, the applicant is not admitted.

The administrator confirms before any admission that the new admission will not exceed licensed capacity. The count includes residents on hospital or leave status who hold a bed, and it is recorded on the screening checklist.

The administrator or on-site manager makes the admission decision and records it in writing with the date, the reasons and their signature. If the applicant is declined, the administrator tells the applicant and representative in writing within [NUMBER] business days and gives the reason. The community can suggest other appropriate options, such as a different level of care.
After a decision to admit, the admission agreement is reviewed and signed under RR-02. The agreement includes the written discharge and transfer procedure required by ADM-03.
The resident's assessment and care plan follow under ADM-02. The care plan is completed within 14 days of admission.

Retention review: the administrator or on-site manager reviews each resident's continued eligibility at every reassessment under ADM-02 and whenever a change in condition occurs (HLT-01). The review asks whether the resident now needs continuous medical or nursing care, restraints, isolation or confinement for behavior, or can no longer take part in transfers.

If the review shows the community can no longer safely meet the resident's needs, the administrator or on-site manager contacts the representative or legal surrogate and starts the transfer process in ADM-03. The review is documented in the record. The community does not hold a resident past the point it can safely care for them.
The administrator keeps declined-applicant screening records for [NUMBER] years. Admitted residents' screening documents are filed in the resident record under REC-01.
The administrator reviews screening decisions, including those that were declined, in the quarterly quality review (ALC-12) to check that criteria are applied consistently.

responsibilities.duty: Performs and documents the pre-admission evaluation; runs the sex offender registry inquiry or obtains the fingerprint check; documents added safety measures; confirms capacity; makes and signs the admission decision; reviews retention at every reassessment and change in condition.
Gathers information and completes the checklist under the administrator's direction. May not make the final decision.
Provides accurate health and history information and the physician examination form.
Approves these admission criteria and makes sure the community does not admit or keep residents needing more care than it is authorized or able to provide.

documentation: Admission Screening Checklist signed and dated by the administrator or on-site manager
Physician examination on the DCH-required form, including TB status
National Sex Offender Registry inquiry result or fingerprint check result
Written added safety measures for registered sex offenders or violent offenders, where applicable
Written admission or decline decision with reasons and notice to the applicant
Capacity count on the date of admission
Retention review notes at each reassessment or change in condition

policies.category: Admission, Retention and Discharge
policies.title: Resident Assessment, Reassessment and Care Plan
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Community (ALC, Ch. 111-8-63). A PCH adopts the same assessment and care plan procedures as agency policy to the extent consistent with Ch. 111-8-62.
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident's needs and preferences are assessed in writing, that a care plan is in place within 14 days of admission, and that it is kept current so care matches the resident's actual condition.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a resident needs assessment for every resident. The assessment covers family supports, ADL function, physical care needs, medical information, cognitive and behavioral impairments and the resident's preferences (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.17(2)). A written care plan is completed within 14 days of admission. The plan is updated at least annually, whenever the resident's needs change substantially, and when the resident is assigned to a memory care center (.17(3)). In a certified memory care center, residents are reassessed at the triggers set out in the center's written description, which come before the customary quarterly review (.19). An assistive device (such as a walker or a bedrail used as a mobility aid) is used only when a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant has ordered it, the care plan describes its use, and the resident has consented. The resident or representative takes part in developing the care plan and signs it. The community provides assisted living with protective care and watchful oversight (.17(1)). It provides periodic or short-term medical and nursing services only as ADM-01 and HLT-03 allow. Any such services are purchased by the resident unless they fall in an exception, which is care planning, training, medication administration and competency checks (.17(11)).

definitions.definition: The written evaluation of the resident's family supports, ADL function, physical care, medical information, cognitive and behavioral impairments and preferences.
The written plan that describes the services, supervision and assistance each resident will receive and who provides them.
A change in condition that alters the services or supervision the resident needs, such as a hospitalization, a new diagnosis, a significant decline in function or a new behavior.
A device used to support function or mobility. As defined in the licensing rules, it requires a physician, NP or PA order, a written care plan and resident consent.
An event that requires a new assessment in a memory care center before the customary quarterly review, as listed in the center's written description.

procedures: The administrator or on-site manager assigns each new admission to a staff member trained to complete the needs assessment. The staff member is named on the assessment form.

On the day of admission, the assigned staff member begins the needs assessment with the resident and representative, using the DCH-required physician examination, the pre-admission screening and the family's input. The form is completed no later than [NUMBER] days after admission.

The assessment documents each of the following: family and other supports; ADL function (bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, eating, mobility); physical care needs; medical information, including diagnoses, allergies and medications; cognitive and behavioral impairments; and the resident's preferences for routine, food, activities and privacy.
The assessment records assisted-self-preservation ability, so that staffing under ALC-02 can be set accordingly.
The administrator or on-site manager reviews the assessment for completeness within [NUMBER] business days and signs it. Gaps are corrected before the care plan is finalized.

The care plan is drafted from the assessment and is completed within 14 days of admission. It names the services, who provides them, how often, and any supervision or safety measures. It also records the resident's choices and preferences.
