If an assistive device is needed, staff obtain the written order from the physician, NP or PA, describe the device and its use in the care plan, and get the resident's consent before the device is used. If an order or consent is missing, the device is not used. A device that would restrict movement is handled under SAF-02.

The resident or the representative or legal surrogate reviews the care plan with the staff member, asks questions and signs and dates it. If the resident or representative declines to sign, staff record the refusal and the reason.

The care plan is kept in the resident's record and a summary of the tasks assigned to each direct care staff member is available to the staff on each shift. Staff are told of any change on the day it is made.
The care plan is reviewed at least annually. The annual review is scheduled at admission and tracked on the community's calendar. The assessment is redone at the annual review.

If a resident has a substantial change in condition, staff notify the administrator or on-site manager on the same day. The administrator arranges a new assessment and updates the care plan promptly, within [NUMBER] days at most, and tells the resident, representative and direct care staff of the changes.

A resident who is moved into a certified memory care center is reassessed before or at the time of assignment. The care plan is updated as part of the move (see HLT-02). The center's written reassessment triggers are applied from that point on.

In a memory care center, the staff reassess when a trigger in the written description occurs, before the customary quarterly review. Triggers might include a fall, a wandering or elopement event, a significant behavior change or a hospitalization. The reassessment and any care plan change are documented the same day.
At each reassessment the administrator or on-site manager re-checks retention eligibility under ADM-01. If needs exceed what the community can provide, the transfer procedure in ADM-03 starts.

Where a resident needs periodic or short-term nursing or medical services beyond what the community provides, staff tell the resident and representative that such services are purchased by the resident (for example, through a home health agency or hospice), and they coordinate under HLT-04. The care plan notes which provider is responsible.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns assessors; reviews and signs assessments; makes sure care plans are completed within 14 days, updated at least annually and on change; applies retention review.
Completes the needs assessment and drafts the care plan with the resident and representative.
Follow the care plan, report changes in the resident's condition the same day and record the care provided.
Takes part in the assessment and the care plan, and signs the plan.
Orders assistive devices and provides medical information used in the assessment.

documentation: Signed and dated needs assessment covering the six required areas
Care plan completed within 14 days of admission, with resident or representative signature
Annual and change-in-condition care plan updates with dates
Physician, NP or PA order and resident consent for each assistive device
Memory care reassessment records and the trigger that prompted each one
Notes on staff communication of care plan changes

policies.category: Admission, Retention and Discharge
policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Community (ALC, Ch. 111-8-63). A PCH adopts the same procedures as agency policy to the extent consistent with Ch. 111-8-62.
policies.purpose: To make sure every discharge or transfer is planned, safe and respects the resident's rights, with proper written notice, family involvement, and an orderly handoff of medications, records and belongings.
policies.policy: Every admission agreement includes a written procedure for discharge and transfer (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.29(1)). When a discharge or transfer is needed, the administrator or on-site manager contacts the representative or legal surrogate. [AGENCY NAME] gives 30 days' written notice of its intent to discharge or transfer a resident unless an immediate transfer is required, for example, because of an emergency or a sudden change in condition under HLT-01 (.26). A resident who has no court commitment and no authorized representative may self-discharge on 30 days' written notice to the community (.25(u)). Refunds and final settlement are made as the admission agreement provides. At discharge or transfer, [AGENCY NAME] sends the resident's medications, records and personal property with the resident or to the receiving provider. [AGENCY NAME] does not punish or harass a resident for exercising rights, including the right to challenge a discharge (.25).

definitions.definition: The end of a resident's stay when the resident leaves the community, whether by the resident's choice or the community's decision.
A move to another setting, such as a hospital, nursing home, memory care center or other community.
A transfer that must occur without 30 days' notice because of an emergency or sudden adverse change.
A resident's own decision to leave. It is available on 30 days' written notice to a resident who has no court commitment and no authorized representative.
The person authorized to act for the resident, such as a health care agent or guardian, as documented in the record (see RR-04).

procedures: Each admission agreement is reviewed with the resident and representative at signing. It includes the written discharge and transfer procedure, the 30-day notice requirement, the self-discharge provision and the refund terms (see RR-02).
When a resident's needs may no longer be met, or another reason for discharge or transfer arises, the staff member who identified it tells the administrator or on-site manager the same day.

The administrator or on-site manager reviews the situation using the latest assessment and care plan (ADM-02) and consults the resident's physician as needed. The decision and the reasons are written and dated.

The administrator or on-site manager contacts the representative or legal surrogate (and the resident) promptly, in person or by phone, and records the date, time and person contacted. They discuss the reason and options for care elsewhere.

The administrator provides written notice of intent to discharge or transfer at least 30 days before the planned date, unless an immediate transfer is required. The notice states the reason, the date, the options and the resident's right to contact the Long-Term Care Ombudsman (RR-01). The notice is delivered by hand or by mail, and a copy is kept in the record.

Staff help the resident and family find an appropriate new setting. They share the resident's current information with the receiving provider with the resident's or representative's consent (RR-05). They coordinate the transport and move date.

For an immediate transfer, staff follow HLT-01 first: make the emergency call, notify the representative, and send emergency information with the resident. The administrator provides written notice of the transfer to the representative as soon as practical, and the reason for the immediacy is documented.

If a resident wants to leave, staff tell the administrator at once. Where the resident has no court commitment and no authorized representative, the resident gives 30 days' written notice. Staff help prepare the notice if asked. If the resident or the representative sets an earlier date, the administrator records that agreement in writing.

Staff do not threaten discharge to stop a resident from complaining, using the grievance process or enforcing a right (RR-01, ALC-06). Any suggestion that a discharge was retaliation is reviewed by the administrator and the governing body.

Before the move, the nurse or certified staff member who handles medications reconciles the medication supply and orders. Medications belonging to the resident are released to the resident, representative or receiving provider with a signed receipt, following ALC-07 or PCH-06.

Resident records needed for continued care, such as medication list, care plan, diagnoses, contacts, advance directives and DNR, are copied and sent with the resident or to the receiving provider with authorization. The original record stays in the community under REC-01.

Resident funds and valuables are accounted for and returned with a signed receipt under RR-03. Personal property is inventoried against the admission inventory and returned. Anything left behind is secured and the resident or representative is told in writing how and when to collect it.

The business office calculates the final account and any refund according to the admission agreement. It issues a written settlement statement to the resident or representative within [NUMBER] days of the discharge date and sends any refund owed within that period.
If the resident dies, the procedures in HLT-04 apply, and the settlement is made with the legal representative or estate.

The administrator completes a discharge summary that records the date, reason, notices given, destination, items released and settlement. It is filed in the record. Any serious incident connected to the transfer is reported under REC-02.
The administrator reviews discharges and transfers quarterly in the quality review (ALC-12) to look for patterns, such as many transfers for one reason.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on discharge or transfer, contacts the representative or legal surrogate, issues the 30-day written notice, and oversees the transition and settlement.
Reconcile and release medications with a signed receipt.
Calculates refunds and issues the final account statement.
Help the resident prepare for the move, and protect the resident's belongings and dignity.
Receives notice, takes part in the planning and gives any required written notice of self-discharge.

documentation: Signed admission agreement showing the written discharge and transfer procedure
Written 30-day notice of discharge or transfer, or documentation of why an immediate transfer was needed
Log of contacts with the representative or legal surrogate
Resident's written 30-day self-discharge notice, where applicable
Medication release receipt
Property and funds return receipts and final settlement statement
Discharge summary filed in the resident record
Record of transfer information sent to the receiving provider

policies.category: Health and Care Services
policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Community (ALC, Ch. 111-8-63). A PCH adopts the same procedures as agency policy to the extent consistent with Ch. 111-8-62.
policies.purpose: To make sure staff respond immediately to an accident or sudden adverse change, call the right people in the right order, honor each resident's advance directives, and report as required to the representative and to DCH.
policies.policy: When a resident has an accident or a sudden adverse change in condition, [AGENCY NAME] staff act immediately, notify the representative or legal surrogate, and record the change and the response in the resident's file (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.26). If a resident is unresponsive, staff follow this order. If the resident is a hospice enrollee, call the hospice, then the health care agent, then EMS and start CPR if there is no DNR order. If there is a valid DNR order, staff honor it in good faith. If the resident has a health care agent under O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq., staff call the agent, and if the agent cannot be reached and there is no DNR, staff call EMS and start CPR. If there is no hospice, DNR or directive, staff call EMS and start CPR unless the resident is clearly dead or CPR is clearly futile and no physician, authorized RN or PA is on site. Staff have ready access to emergency numbers and resident information at all times, including during transport. The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of any accident, injury or death, reports to the representative or legal surrogate, and keeps copies in the resident file and in a central quality-assurance file. [AGENCY NAME] reports a serious injury requiring medical attention, and the other serious incidents listed in .30, to DCH within 24 hours (.30). The admission agreement provides for continuous assessment of residents and for referral or transfer when a resident's condition changes.

definitions.definition: A sudden or significant change in a resident's physical, mental or behavioral status, or an accident or injury.
An injury that requires medical attention. It includes a pressure ulcer that has not been properly cared for, as the rules define injury.
A valid do-not-resuscitate order in the resident's record.
The person named under a health care directive under O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq. to make health decisions for the resident (see RR-04).
The face sheet, medication list, allergies, diagnoses, advance directive or DNR, physician and representative contacts. It travels with the resident.

procedures: Any staff member who sees an accident, an injury or a sudden adverse change stays with the resident, checks responsiveness and breathing, and calls for help. If the resident is unresponsive or the situation is life-threatening, staff follow steps 3 to 7 without waiting for a supervisor.
A staff member notifies the administrator or on-site manager immediately. If neither is on site, the staff member calls the on-call number posted at each station ([PHONE]).

First check the resident record (face sheet or emergency information packet) for a hospice enrollment, a valid DNR order or a health care directive naming an agent. These documents are kept in a standard place that every shift knows.
Hospice enrollee: call the hospice first and follow its direction. Then call the health care agent. If there is no DNR, call EMS and start CPR.
Valid DNR: honor it in good faith. Do not start CPR. Call the hospice or physician and the representative and stay with the resident. Keep the resident comfortable.
Health care agent but no hospice or DNR: call the agent. If the agent cannot be reached and there is no DNR, call EMS and start CPR.

No hospice, DNR or directive: call EMS and start CPR unless the resident is clearly dead or CPR is clearly futile and no physician, authorized RN or PA is on site to make that call. Staff trained in CPR continue until EMS takes over.

For non-emergency changes, such as a new confusion, fall without apparent injury, decreased intake, fever or new skin problem, staff call the resident's physician or the physician's office the same day. They follow the instructions and record them.

The staff member or administrator notifies the representative or legal surrogate immediately for an accident or sudden adverse change, and as soon as possible for other changes. The notice is recorded with date, time, person called and what was said.

If the resident goes to the hospital, a staff member sends the emergency information packet with the resident, including current medications, allergies, diagnoses, advance directive or DNR, and contacts. If staff go in the vehicle or follow in a car, they carry the staff emergency number list.

A staff member records the change and the response in the resident file: what was observed, time, who was called, actions taken, EMS arrival and the outcome. Entries are signed and dated. The shift supervisor passes the change to the next shift.

The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of any accident, injury or death. The investigation interviews witnesses, reviews the care plan and conditions, and identifies what can prevent a repeat. The findings are written down.
The administrator reports the findings to the representative or legal surrogate and places copies in the resident file and in the central quality-assurance file.

The administrator decides within 24 hours whether the event is a serious incident. DCH must be told within 24 hours of the incident, or of reasonable cause to believe one occurred, if it was a serious injury needing medical attention, an accidental or unanticipated death not tied to the natural course of illness, an assault, battery, abuse, neglect or exploitation, or another event listed in .30. The report is made under REC-02.

The DCH report names the community and administrator, the incident date and discovery date, the type of incident with a brief description, and the immediate corrective or preventive action. A copy is kept in the central file. The administrator cooperates with any DCH complaint investigation.

After any change in condition, the care plan is reviewed and updated if needs have substantially changed (ADM-02). The administrator also reviews whether the resident can still be kept in the community (ADM-01) and, if not, starts ADM-03.
Each year, the administrator verifies that staff know where emergency numbers and resident information are kept, and has staff practice the emergency order of calls during training (ALC-04).

responsibilities.duty: Respond immediately, follow the call order, summon EMS where required and start CPR when it applies, and report to the administrator or on-site manager.
Directs the response, notifies the representative, starts the investigation, decides on DCH reporting and keeps the central quality-assurance file.
Makes sure the emergency packet goes with the resident and that the change is handed off at shift change.

responsibilities.role: Physician, hospice or health care agent
responsibilities.duty: Give direction on care, and decisions on resuscitation and treatment, according to the resident's directives.

documentation: Resident file entry of the change and the response, signed and dated
Log of notifications to the representative or legal surrogate
Physician and hospice contact notes
Investigation findings kept in the resident file and in the central quality-assurance file
DCH serious incident report (within 24 hours) and proof of submission
Emergency information packet sent with the resident
Care plan updates following the change

policies.category: Health and Care Services
policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care (Certified Memory Care Centers)
policies.applies_to: Any ALC or PCH that holds itself out as providing specialized dementia care or charges more for it. Ch. 111-8-63 requirements are applied in the ALC. A PCH follows the PCH memory care process with DCH.
policies.purpose: To make sure that memory care is offered only under a current DCH certificate, that staffing, training and the physical program meet the rules, and that residents with dementia receive safe, dignified and appropriate care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not operate a memory care center, and does not hold itself out as providing specialized dementia care or charge more for it, without a current DCH memory care certificate (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-62-.05 for PCHs; 111-8-63-.19 for ALCs). The certificate fee is $200 per year (DCH Schedule of Licensure Activity Fees). An ALC must hold a current ALC permit before applying for the certificate. The licensed residential care profile carries a written description of the center covering philosophy; how services differ from the rest of the community; staffing and training; admission and screening criteria; assessment and reassessment triggers that come before the customary quarterly review; staffing patterns; physical environment and security; activities; fees; discharge criteria; emergency procedures; and family involvement (.19). Staffing is at least one dementia-trained direct care staff member per 12 residents in waking hours and per 15 in non-waking hours, measured as a monthly average. A registered nurse or licensed practical nurse is present in the center for 8 hours per week for 1 to 12 residents, 16 for 13 to 30, 24 for 31 to 40 and 40 for more than 40 (.19). Under O.C.G.A. 31-7-12.4, all staff receive at least 4 hours of dementia-specific orientation within the first 30 days. Direct care staff complete at least 16 hours of dementia training within the first 30 days of working independently with residents with dementia, and at least 8 hours every year after that. The center does not use chemical or physical restraints to control behavior.

definitions.definition: A distinct part of the community that provides specialized care for residents with Alzheimer's disease or other dementia and holds a DCH memory care certificate.
A direct care staff member who has completed the dementia training required by O.C.G.A. 31-7-12.4.
The hours of the day set out in the center's written description. Waking hours are [WAKING HOURS]. Non-waking hours are [NON-WAKING HOURS].
The staffing ratio is measured as an average across the calendar month, calculated from the center's actual schedules and census.
An event named in the written description that requires reassessment before the customary quarterly review.
A physical or chemical restraint as the licensing rules define it. Examples are bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking, and mitts. Alarm wristbands are not restraints.

procedures: Before offering memory care, the governing body and administrator confirm the community has a current permit and the DCH memory care certificate for the memory care center. For an ALC, the current ALC permit is confirmed first. For a PCH, the administrator follows the PCH memory care process with DCH. No resident is admitted to the center before the certificate is issued.
The administrator pays the $200 annual certificate fee on time and calendars the renewal date. The certificate is posted with the permit under GOV-01.

The administrator maintains the written 12-element description of the center and keeps it current with the licensed residential care profile. The description covers each of these elements: philosophy; how services differ; staffing and training; admission and screening criteria; assessment and reassessment triggers; staffing patterns; physical environment and security; activities; fees; discharge criteria; emergency procedures; family involvement.
The description is given to every prospective resident and representative before admission and is available to staff. Any change is made in writing, with DCH notified as required.

Admission to the center follows the screening criteria in the written description and ADM-01. The administrator confirms that the resident has a physician diagnosis or documentation supporting the need for memory care.
On assignment to the center, the resident is reassessed and the care plan is updated (ADM-02). The representative is told in writing of the move and of the fee.

The administrator sets the daily staffing schedule so there is at least one dementia-trained direct care staff member for every 12 residents during waking hours and for every 15 during non-waking hours. The administrator calculates the monthly average from the schedule at month end and records it.

The administrator arranges RN or LPN hours in the center: 8 hours per week for 1 to 12 residents, 16 for 13 to 30, 24 for 31 to 40, and 40 for more than 40. The nurse signs a log of hours worked in the center each week. If the census moves to a higher band, the schedule is adjusted immediately.
Every staff member who works in the center, including non-direct care staff, receives at least 4 hours of dementia-specific orientation within their first 30 days (ALC-04).

Each direct care staff member completes at least 16 hours of dementia training within 30 days of beginning to work independently with residents with dementia, and at least 8 hours every year after that. Staff who have not completed the 16 hours do not work alone with residents in the center and are not counted as dementia-trained in the ratio.
The administrator keeps documentation of every dementia course: content, instructor qualifications, agenda and attendance roster signed by participants.

Staff apply the written reassessment triggers. When a trigger occurs, such as a fall, an elopement attempt, a major behavior change or a hospitalization, the nurse reassesses the resident before the next quarterly review and updates the care plan.

Staff use person-centered, non-drug approaches to behaviors first. Chemical or physical restraints are not used for behavioral control. If a staff member believes a resident needs something that would restrict movement or sedate, the staff member calls the administrator, who follows SAF-02. A resident who needs restraints is not appropriate for the center and is handled under ADM-03.
Staff keep the center's physical environment and security features working, check them every shift and report problems to the administrator. Wandering and missing-resident procedures follow SAF-01.
Daily activities fit the residents' abilities and preferences and are described in the written description. The activity staff record who took part (DL-02).
The administrator invites family involvement as described in the written description, such as care plan meetings and family education, and records contacts.
The administrator reviews the center's staffing average, nurse hours, training status and incidents each quarter in the quality review (ALC-12).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the memory care program and makes sure the community holds a current certificate before operating it.
Maintains the certificate, pays the fee, keeps the 12-element description current, schedules staff to meet ratios, arranges nurse hours and keeps training records.

responsibilities.role: RN or LPN assigned to the center
responsibilities.duty: Provides and logs the required weekly hours; performs reassessments and advises on care plans.
Provide care in line with the care plan, use non-drug approaches and report changes.
Provide daily programming suited to residents with dementia.
Take part in care planning and receive the written description and fee information.

documentation: Current DCH memory care certificate and payment record for the $200 annual fee
Written 12-element description of the center and proof of delivery to residents and representatives
Daily schedules and monthly staffing average calculation
RN or LPN weekly hours log
Dementia training records: course content, instructor qualifications, agendas and signed rosters
Reassessment records and the trigger for each
Care plans updated on assignment to the center
Activity attendance records and family contact log

policies.category: Health and Care Services
policies.title: Falls Prevention and Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Community (ALC, Ch. 111-8-63). A PCH adopts the same procedures as agency policy to the extent consistent with Ch. 111-8-62.
policies.purpose: To reduce falls and pressure injuries, and to make sure that when they happen they are cared for, investigated and reported correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] screens every resident for fall risk at admission and again after any fall or change in condition, and updates the care plan when needs change (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.17(3)). The licensing rules define injury to include pressure ulcers that are not properly cared for (.03), so [AGENCY NAME] treats pressure ulcers as reportable events and checks skin regularly. A fall that causes a serious injury requiring medical attention is investigated immediately and reported to DCH within 24 hours (.26 and .30, with .30 covered under REC-02). An assistive device, such as a walker, cane or wheelchair used for mobility support, is used only with a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant order, a written care plan and the resident's consent (.03). [AGENCY NAME] does not use bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking or mitts to prevent falls unless they meet the rules in SAF-02. Alarm wristbands are not restraints. Limited nursing services, meaning care completed within 7 days or provided intermittently, are provided only as the licensing rules allow and as set out in ADM-02 (.17(11)).

definitions.definition: Any unplanned descent to the floor or other surface, with or without injury, whether seen by staff or found.
An area of skin or underlying tissue damaged by pressure. A pressure ulcer that is not properly cared for is an injury under the licensing rules.
An injury that requires medical attention and is reportable to DCH within 24 hours.
A device that supports mobility or function. It requires an order, a written care plan and the resident's consent.
A physical or chemical restraint as defined in the licensing rules. Bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking and mitts count as restraints. Alarm wristbands do not.
Nursing care that is completed within 7 days or provided intermittently.

procedures: At admission, the nurse or designated trained staff member completes a fall risk screening and a skin check with the resident and records them with the needs assessment (ADM-02). The screening looks at fall history, gait and balance, medications, vision, footwear, continence, cognition and environment.

The screening result and any interventions are written in the care plan, which is completed within 14 days of admission. Interventions might include supervision, scheduled toileting, a medication review by the physician, better lighting, non-slip footwear or an assistive device.

Before an assistive device is used, staff obtain the order from the physician, NP or PA, describe the device and its use in the care plan and get the resident's consent. Staff do not provide or require a device without all three.

Staff do not use bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking or mitts as a falls intervention without following SAF-02. If a family or resident asks for one, staff refer the request to the administrator.

Direct care staff check each resident's skin during bathing and dressing and report any redness, open area, blister or bruise to the nurse or administrator on the same shift. The finding is recorded with the date, location and description.

For residents at risk of pressure injury, such as those who are bedbound, in a chair most of the day or incontinent, the care plan sets out repositioning, pressure relief, hygiene, nutrition and hydration steps. Staff carry them out and record them.

When a pressure ulcer or open skin area is found, the administrator or nurse notifies the physician the same day, obtains orders and updates the care plan. The resident or family is told. If treatment needs a nurse, it is obtained as the rules allow, such as through a home health agency or hospice (HLT-04), and staff follow the orders.

When a resident falls, staff do not move the resident until they have checked for injury. They call for help and, if there is a possible serious injury or the resident is unresponsive, follow HLT-01 and call EMS.

After any fall, staff notify the administrator or on-site manager at once, notify the representative or legal surrogate, and call the physician for any injury or change in condition. Staff record the fall in the resident file: time, place, what happened, injuries, who was told and actions taken.

The administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause of a fall that results in injury and reports to the representative or legal surrogate (.26). Copies go in the resident file and in the central quality-assurance file.

If a fall results in a serious injury requiring medical attention, or if a pressure ulcer was not properly cared for and meets the definition of injury, the administrator reports it to DCH within 24 hours under REC-02, with the required contents: names, incident and discovery dates, type and description and the immediate corrective or preventive action.

After every fall, the nurse or administrator re-screens fall risk and updates the care plan within [NUMBER] days, or immediately if the fall caused a substantial change in the resident's needs. Staff on every shift are told of the changes.

If a resident falls repeatedly or declines, the administrator reviews whether the resident still meets retention criteria (ADM-01) and whether more care or a different level of care is needed (ADM-03).
Maintenance staff check floors, lighting, grab bars, handrails and walkways in each area weekly. Hazards such as spills or loose rugs are fixed immediately. Corridors are kept clear (DL-03, SAF-03).

If a resident needs nursing care that is limited, such as a short course of wound care completed within 7 days, the administrator confirms with the physician and the home health provider how it will be done, and records the arrangement in the care plan.

The administrator reviews all falls and pressure injuries each quarter in the quality review (ALC-12). The review looks at times, places and causes and the effect of interventions, and changes the program as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Investigates falls with injury, reports to the representative and to DCH, and reviews retention and trends.
Completes fall and skin screenings, advises on care plans and follows up on orders.
Carry out fall and skin interventions, check skin during care and report falls and skin changes the same shift.
Keep floors, lighting, handrails and grab bars in safe condition.
Orders assistive devices and treatment for skin problems and injuries.

documentation: Admission and post-fall fall-risk screenings
Skin checks and records of repositioning and pressure relief
Physician, NP or PA order and resident consent for each assistive device
Fall record in the resident file with notifications
Investigation findings in the resident file and the central quality-assurance file
DCH report within 24 hours for serious injuries
Care plan updates after falls or skin changes
Quarterly falls and skin review notes

policies.category: Health and Care Services
policies.title: Hospice, Home Health, Nursing Services and Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Communities (Ch. 111-8-63) and Personal Care Homes (Ch. 111-8-62). Written to the ALC standards; a PCH applies the same practices together with the parallel requirements of Ch. 111-8-62.
policies.purpose: To make clear which nursing and medical services [AGENCY NAME] provides and which the resident purchases, to coordinate safely with hospice and home health providers, and to set out what staff do when a resident is unresponsive or dies, including investigation, DCH reporting, family notice and refunds.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides assisted living, protective care and watchful oversight (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.17). Periodic or short-term medical and nursing services are not community services. The resident purchases them from a provider of the resident's choice. The exceptions are care planning, staff training, medication administration and competency checks, which the community performs as part of its own operations (111-8-63-.17(11)). The community cooperates with hospice and home health providers so that services are coordinated, safe and consistent with the resident's care plan, and so that the resident's directives are honored. When a resident is unresponsive or dies, staff act immediately and follow the sequence in 111-8-63-.26. The community reports and investigates any accidental or unanticipated death that is not tied to the natural course of illness, and reports it to DCH within 24 hours (111-8-63-.26 and .30). Refunds after a death follow the admission agreement (111-8-63-.16). Hospice residents' liquid morphine on site is limited to 50 ml per resident (111-8-63-.20).

definitions.definition: A resident who has elected hospice care and is served by a licensed hospice provider under the resident's hospice plan of care.
Periodic or short-term nursing or medical services delivered to a resident by a licensed provider chosen and paid for by the resident, rather than by the community.
An accidental death or a death not tied to the natural course of the resident's illness. It triggers an immediate investigation and a 24-hour report to DCH.
A valid Do Not Resuscitate order that staff must honor in good faith.
The person appointed under an advance directive for health care (O.C.G.A. 31-32-1 et seq.) to make health care decisions for the resident.

procedures: Before admission and at each reassessment, the administrator or on-site manager identifies which nursing or medical needs are periodic or short-term. The admission agreement and care plan state that the resident purchases these services from a provider of the resident's choice.
The community does not hold itself out as providing continuous medical or nursing care. If a resident's needs exceed what the community may retain, the administrator starts the process in ADM-03.

When a resident enrolls with hospice or engages a home health agency, the administrator obtains a copy of the provider's name, 24-hour contact number, plan of care and current orders and files them in the resident record.

The administrator or designee meets with the hospice or home health case manager within [NUMBER OF] business days of the start of services to agree on who does what. The community's role is limited to assisted living services, and provider staff perform the clinical tasks.
The care plan is updated to include hospice or home health services, the resident's directives and the provider's visit schedule. Staff are told what they must observe and report to the provider.
Hospice and home health staff sign in on arrival and out on departure. They report any change they observe to the on-duty supervisor.

Medications for hospice residents follow ALC-07 (or PCH-06 in a PCH). Orders are required for all medications. Only certified medication aides administer medications in an ALC. The administrator ensures that no more than 50 ml of liquid morphine is kept for any one hospice resident. All controlled substances are kept in a locked cabinet or box of substantial construction with a daily-updated log.

When a resident is found unresponsive, the staff member calls for the supervisor and checks the resident file for hospice enrollment, a DNR and an advance directive. These must be readily available at the point of care.

If the resident is a hospice enrollee: staff call the hospice first, then the health care agent, then EMS and start CPR if there is no DNR. If a valid DNR is in the file, staff honor it in good faith.
If the resident has a health care agent: staff call the agent. If the agent cannot be reached and there is no DNR, staff call EMS and start CPR.

If the resident has no hospice enrollment, DNR or directive: staff call EMS and start CPR. The only exception is where CPR is clearly futile and no physician, authorized registered nurse or physician assistant is on site.
Staff keep emergency numbers and resident information at the point of care and send the face sheet, medication list and directives with the resident during transport.
On any accident or sudden adverse change, staff act immediately, notify the resident's representative or legal surrogate, and record the change and the response in the resident file.

When a resident dies, the supervisor notifies the physician or hospice, the representative or legal surrogate and the administrator. Staff do not move or release the body except as directed by hospice, the physician, EMS, law enforcement or the coroner, and then only to the funeral home designated by the family or in the resident's written instructions.

The administrator secures the resident's room, medications and personal property under RR-03. Controlled substances and other medications are inventoried and disposed of under ALC-07. Staff use the community's release-of-property form and obtain a signed receipt from the person receiving the belongings.

If the death was accidental or unanticipated, the administrator or on-site manager starts an immediate investigation of the cause. The administrator reports the death to DCH within 24 hours of the incident or of reasonable cause to believe it occurred, giving the community and administrator names, the incident date and discovery date, the incident type and a brief description, and the immediate corrective or preventive action taken. The report goes through [DCH REPORTING METHOD PER CURRENT DCH INSTRUCTIONS].
The administrator reports the investigation findings to the representative or legal surrogate and keeps copies in the resident file and in the central quality-assurance file.

The business office calculates any refund under the refund provisions of the signed admission agreement (111-8-63-.16) and sends the refund and an itemized statement to the person entitled to it, as stated in the agreement. Room-and-board and personal-service charges are handled as the agreement provides.
The administrator reviews each death at the next quality-assurance meeting for trends and corrective action (ALC-12 or PCH-11).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure hospice and home health coordination, run the immediate investigation of any unanticipated death, make the 24-hour DCH report, and report to the representative or legal surrogate.
Check directives and hospice status, call the right people in the right order, start CPR when required, and document the response.
Keep controlled substances secured and logged, ensure the 50 ml liquid morphine limit per hospice resident, and inventory medications after a death.
Issue refunds and final statements according to the admission agreement.
Deliver clinical services under their own plans of care and report changes to the community.

documentation: Hospice or home health agreement, provider contacts, plan of care and orders in the resident record
Updated care plan reflecting external services
DNR, advance directive and health care agent information readily available in the resident file
Change-of-condition notes with notification times
Controlled substance log and medication inventory after death
Incident report, investigation record and representative notice, copied to the resident file and the central quality-assurance file
DCH 24-hour report and confirmation of submission
Property release receipt and refund calculation
Quality-assurance review minutes

policies.category: Safety and Protection
policies.title: Elopement, Missing Resident and Mattie's Call
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Communities and Personal Care Homes
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk of residents leaving the community unsafely, and to ensure a fast, coordinated search and the required law-enforcement and DCH reports when a resident is missing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies residents at risk of wandering or elopement, protects them without locking them in or restricting their free access to common areas, and keeps a current photo and description of each at-risk resident. When staff have actual knowledge that a resident is missing, they begin a search at once and the community calls local police within 30 minutes under the Mattie's Call Act. The community reports the start and the end of a Mattie's Call to DCH within 30 minutes of the contact with law enforcement (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.30). A missing resident who is injured, or whose absence otherwise meets a serious-incident category, is also reported to DCH within 24 hours (111-8-63-.30). The community does not lock a resident into or out of a bedroom or restrict a resident's free access to common areas.

definitions.definition: Georgia's statewide alert for a missing person with a disability or cognitive impairment, activated through law enforcement. In Ch. 111-8-63-.03, a Mattie's-call-related elopement is an elopement that results in a Mattie's Call.
A resident leaving the community or its grounds without staff knowledge, or without the supervision the care plan requires.
The point at which any staff member knows, or has been told, that the resident cannot be found after a reasonable initial check.
A resident whose assessment, behavior history, diagnosis or exit-seeking shows a risk of wandering or leaving unsafely.

procedures: At pre-admission screening, admission and every reassessment, the administrator or designee screens each resident for wandering and elopement risk, using the assessment (ADM-02), family and prior-provider information and staff observation. The result is recorded in the resident record.

For every at-risk resident, the community keeps a current color photo and a written description (height, weight, hair, clothing usually worn, medical conditions, likely destinations, how the resident communicates). The photo and description are updated at least [NUMBER OF] months and after any significant change in appearance. Copies are kept in the central location staff can reach immediately.

The care plan states the specific supervision and prevention measures for each at-risk resident. Measures may include increased checks, door alarms or chimes, a medical alert system approved by DCH, and engaging activities at times of day when exit-seeking occurs. The resident or representative gives consent to any device. Alarm wristbands are allowed because they do not count as restraints. Staff never lock a resident into or out of a room or restrict access to common areas.

The administrator tests door alarms and any alert devices at least [FREQUENCY] and records each test. Broken equipment is repaired or replaced immediately and extra staff checks are put in place until repaired.
Staff are trained at orientation and at least annually on spotting exit-seeking behavior, the search plan and who calls whom (ALC-04 or PCH-03).
Staff take a head count of at-risk residents at every shift change and at meals, and record it.

When any staff member cannot find a resident, that staff member immediately alerts the supervisor on duty and every other staff member. The supervisor assigns search zones: the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, all floors, outdoor grounds, parking lots, vehicles, nearby streets and water hazards, with the highest-risk areas first.

The supervisor starts the search at once. The supervisor or administrator calls 911 or local police as soon as the resident is not found in the first quick check, and in all cases within 30 minutes of actual knowledge. The supervisor gives the resident's name, photo and description, the time last seen and any known destination.

If law enforcement initiates a Mattie's Call, the administrator or designee notifies DCH of the start of the Mattie's Call within 30 minutes of the contact with law enforcement, using [DCH REPORTING METHOD PER CURRENT DCH INSTRUCTIONS], and records the time and the person contacted.
A staff member remains at a telephone to receive calls and to give police the photo, medication list and face sheet. Staff continue the search until law enforcement says otherwise.

The supervisor notifies the resident's representative or legal surrogate and the physician as soon as possible and keeps them updated, and notifies the administrator immediately if the administrator is not on site.

When the resident is found, staff assess the resident for injury, call EMS if there is any sign of injury or medical distress, and notify the representative and physician. The administrator reports the end of the Mattie's Call to DCH within 30 minutes of the contact with law enforcement that ended it.

If the missing resident was hurt, or the event otherwise falls into a serious-incident category, the administrator also submits the serious incident report to DCH within 24 hours, giving the community and administrator names, the date of the incident and of discovery, the incident type and description, and the immediate corrective or preventive action.

The administrator starts an investigation immediately: how the resident left, which alarms or checks failed, staffing at the time, and the resident's recent changes. The investigation and the family report are kept in the resident file and the central quality-assurance file.

Within [NUMBER OF] days, the care team reassesses the resident and updates the care plan, the supervision level and, if needed, the question of whether the resident can be retained safely (ADM-01 and ADM-03).
The administrator takes corrective action such as repairing equipment, retraining staff or changing the staffing pattern, and presents the event at the next quality-assurance meeting.
The community runs a missing-resident drill at least [FREQUENCY] per year, with at least one on each shift over a [NUMBER OF]-month period, and records the time to complete the search plan.

responsibilities.duty: Oversee risk screening, call or authorize the call to police, make the DCH Mattie's Call and serious-incident reports, lead the investigation and corrective action.
Direct the search, make the first calls to police and family, and hold the photo and description file.
Report a missing resident immediately, take head counts, test and respond to alarms, and follow care-plan supervision.
Test and repair door alarms and exterior security, and keep grounds hazards clear.

documentation: Elopement-risk screening and reassessment in the resident record
Current photo and description for each at-risk resident
Care-plan supervision measures and consent for devices
Alarm and device test log
Head-count records
Missing-resident incident record with times of discovery, police call and family notice
DCH Mattie's Call start and end reports with times
DCH serious incident report where applicable
Investigation findings and corrective action
Drill records and staff training attendance

policies.category: Safety and Protection
policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Communities and Personal Care Homes
policies.purpose: To ensure that [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical or chemical restraints, isolation or confinement, that residents who need them are not admitted or retained, and that staff know the state's definition of a restraint and how to respond to unsafe behavior without one.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a resident who needs physical or chemical restraints, isolation or confinement for behavioral control (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.15(1)). Under 111-8-63-.03, bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking of bedding and mitts are treated as restraints. Alarm wristbands are not. The community does not lock a resident into or out of the bedroom and does not restrict free access to common areas (111-8-63-.17(7)). An assistive device is used only with a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant order, a written care plan and the resident's consent (111-8-63-.03). Staff are trained on alternatives to restraint.

definitions.definition: Any device or practice that restricts a resident's freedom of movement or normal access to the body that the resident cannot easily remove. Under Ch. 111-8-63-.03 this includes bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking of bedding and mitts. Alarm wristbands do not count as restraints.
A drug used to control behavior or restrict movement for staff convenience or discipline, and not to treat a diagnosed condition.
A device that helps a resident with mobility or function. It requires a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant order, a written care plan and the resident's consent.
Placing or keeping a resident apart from others, or locking a resident in or out of a room, to control behavior.

procedures: At pre-admission screening, the administrator or on-site manager evaluates whether the applicant would need a physical or chemical restraint, isolation or confinement for behavioral control. If so, the applicant is not admitted and is referred to a more appropriate setting (ADM-01).

Staff are told in orientation and at least annually that restraints are prohibited and what counts as one, using the definitions in this policy (ALC-04 or PCH-03). Training also covers alternatives, including recognizing triggers, redirection, a calm environment, adjusting routines, pain and toileting checks, and one-to-one engagement.

Staff do not use bedrails, wheelchair safety bars, tight tucking or mitts as a means to restrict movement. If a resident, family member or physician requests one, the staff member refers the request to the administrator, who reviews it against the rule and does not authorize it if it would restrict the resident's movement.

The administrator reviews any proposed assistive device. A device may be used only after the order from a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant is filed, the care plan describes why and how it is used, and the resident (or representative where the rules allow) has consented in writing. If the administrator cannot tell whether a device is a restraint, the administrator asks DCH HFRD for guidance before the device is used.

Staff never lock a resident into or out of a bedroom, never restrict free access to common areas, and never confine a resident as punishment or for staff convenience. Delayed-egress or alarm systems in a certified memory care center follow HLT-02 and the fire code and are described in the care plan.

Medications are given only as ordered by the prescriber for a diagnosed condition. Staff do not ask a prescriber for a medication in order to quiet a resident, and the certified medication aide reports to the supervisor any medication that appears to be sedating a resident beyond its purpose (ALC-07 or PCH-06).
When a resident shows agitation or aggression, staff first use non-physical measures: stay calm, give space, remove triggers, offer a quiet area with a staff member present, and call the supervisor.
If a resident or another person is in immediate danger, staff protect other residents, move away, and call 911. Staff do not apply restraints.

After any such event, the supervisor notifies the representative or legal surrogate and physician, and the administrator investigates, documents antecedents and responses, and reports serious incidents under ALC-09 or PCH-08.

If a resident's behavior shows that the community cannot meet the resident's needs without restraint, isolation or confinement, the administrator starts reassessment and, if needed, a discharge or transfer under ADM-03, giving the notice that applies.

The administrator or the RN consultant inspects resident rooms and common areas at least [FREQUENCY] for devices that could act as restraints, such as improvised bedrails, bed sheets tucked tightly, mitts, belts or locked doors. The inspection is recorded and any finding is corrected immediately.
Any suspected misuse of a restraint is treated as possible abuse, and staff must report it under ALC-09 or PCH-08.
The quality-assurance review includes any restraint-related event and any device approval (ALC-12 or PCH-11).

responsibilities.duty: Screen for restraint need at admission, approve assistive devices only when requirements are met, investigate events and order discharge reassessment when needed.
Use alternatives to restraint, never apply restraints, never lock residents in or out, and report concerns.

responsibilities.role: Certified medication aides and nurse or pharmacist reviewer
responsibilities.duty: Give medications only as ordered and flag any medication used or appearing to be used for behavioral control.
Order assistive devices and, with the community, review behavior-related concerns.

documentation: Pre-admission restraint-need screening
Orders, care plan entries and signed consent for any assistive device
Training records on restraint definitions and alternatives
Room and common-area inspection records
Incident reports and investigation notes for behavioral events
Reassessment and discharge or transfer records if retention was not possible
Quality-assurance review notes

policies.category: Safety and Protection
policies.title: Fire Safety, Physical Plant Safety and Electrical Compliance
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Communities and Personal Care Homes
policies.purpose: To keep the building safe for residents and staff, to maintain the fire, electrical, water and physical-plant documentation DCH requires, and to keep the community ready for an unannounced inspection.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps the interior and exterior clean, in good repair and free of unsafe conditions, keeps entrances, exits, sidewalks and escape routes free of hazards, and keeps its name and house number visible from the street (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.13). The community complies with Ch. 111-8-16 (Disaster Preparedness Plans), posts evacuation maps with marked escape routes on each floor, and keeps a clear accessible emergency route through common areas (111-8-63-.14). The community holds a current State Fire Marshal report showing no violations and stating the capacity load, dated within 12 months of the application, and an electrical compliance form signed by a Georgia-licensed electrician, dated within 6 months of the application. Where the community does not use city or county water, it holds a private water test dated within 6 months of the application. The community keeps a drill and fire equipment inspection log. Communities are inspected without notice, and these records and policies are available for review at any time (DCH ALC Application Checklist).

definitions.definition: The maximum number of residents the State Fire Marshal's report allows in the building. Licensed capacity never exceeds it.
The marked path from any area of the building to a safe exit or area of refuge, including corridors, stairs, doors and exterior walkways.
The DCH form completed and signed by a Georgia-licensed electrician stating that the building's electrical system complies with requirements.

procedures: Before the application is submitted, the administrator requests a State Fire Marshal inspection and confirms that the report shows no violations and states the capacity load. The report must be dated within 12 months of the application submission. Any deficiency is corrected and the building is re-inspected before the report is relied on.

Before the application is submitted, the administrator obtains the electrical compliance form signed by a Georgia-licensed electrician, dated within 6 months of the application, and corrects any item the electrician identifies. If the community is not on city or county water, the administrator obtains a private water test within 6 months of the application and keeps the result.

The administrator files the Fire Marshal report, electrician form and water test in the document-control file (GOV-02) and posts or provides them as GOV-01 requires. The administrator calendars each document's date and renews it when DCH or the State Fire Marshal requires it or before it becomes older than the period DCH will accept.
The community never houses more residents than the licensed capacity and the capacity load on the Fire Marshal report.

The maintenance lead or designee inspects the interior and exterior of the building at least weekly using the safety checklist, covering walkways, steps, handrails, floors, lighting, exits, door hardware, kitchens, grounds, parking lots, and any bedroom or common-area defects. Findings are recorded and repaired on a priority schedule, with hazards fixed or made safe the same day.

Staff keep entrances, exits, sidewalks, corridors and escape routes clear of furniture, equipment, carts, snow, ice, debris and anything else that could block or trip someone. Any staff member who sees a hazard removes it or reports it to the supervisor at once.
The administrator confirms that the community's name and house number are visible from the street, day and night, and repairs or replaces signage that is missing, faded or blocked.

The administrator posts evacuation maps with marked escape routes on each floor, at locations where residents and staff will see them, and updates them whenever the layout changes. A clear accessible emergency route through common areas is maintained at all times.

The disaster plan under Ch. 111-8-16 is readily accessible to staff, residents and families. It names the staff positions responsible for implementing it and for obtaining emergency medical attention (ALC-11 or PCH-10).

Fire drills are held at the frequency and on the shifts required by the State Fire Marshal and Ch. 111-8-16, and each is recorded with date, time, shift, evacuation time, residents needing help and any problems found.

Fire alarms, extinguishers, sprinklers, smoke and carbon-monoxide detectors, emergency lighting and exit signs are inspected and tested by qualified persons at the intervals required by the State Fire Marshal and the manufacturer. Each test is entered in the fire equipment inspection log, which is kept on site.

Staff do not use or allow extension cords as permanent wiring, overloaded outlets, unapproved space heaters or damaged electrical equipment. Any electrical change or repair is made by a licensed electrician, and the administrator reviews whether the electrical compliance form needs to be updated.
Smoking, open flame and candles are handled under the house rules (ALC-05 or PCH-04) and in accordance with the Fire Marshal's requirements.
The community keeps an operable non-pay telephone for staff emergency use and private resident access, and posts emergency numbers by the telephone (111-8-63-.17(6)).

After a fire, a safety event or an external emergency that affects safe operation, the administrator reports it to DCH within 24 hours as a serious incident, and, if residents must relocate, gives timely notice of the relocation address to residents, family contacts, representatives and DCH (ALC-09, REC-02).
The administrator reviews the inspection log, drill records and open repairs at each quality-assurance meeting and corrects any recurring problem.

On an unannounced DCH inspection, the administrator or the person in charge makes the Fire Marshal report, electrician form, drill log, equipment log and these policies available to the surveyor immediately.

responsibilities.duty: Obtain and keep current the Fire Marshal report, electrician form and water test, keep the community within licensed capacity and capacity load, and make records available to surveyors.
Perform weekly inspections, arrange repairs and tests, and keep the fire equipment inspection log.
Keep escape routes clear, report hazards and take part in drills.

responsibilities.role: Georgia-licensed electrician and State Fire Marshal
responsibilities.duty: Provide the independent compliance forms and reports the community relies on.

documentation: State Fire Marshal report with capacity load
Electrician compliance form
Private water test results where applicable
Weekly safety inspection checklists and repair records
Fire drill log and fire equipment inspection log
Posted evacuation maps (dated and updated)
Photo or record of street name and house number visibility check
Serious incident reports for fire or emergency events
Document-control index with expiration dates

policies.category: Daily Living
policies.title: Food Service, Menus and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Communities and Personal Care Homes
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives safe, nutritious and well-balanced meals on a reliable schedule, that therapeutic diets are provided as ordered, and that menus are planned, posted and kept as the rules require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] serves at least 3 regularly scheduled, well-balanced meals each day, 7 days a week, and provides therapeutic diets as ordered by the resident's healthcare provider (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.21). No more than 14 hours pass between the evening meal and the morning meal. Nutrition meets the Recommended Daily Diet Allowances, and at least one nutritious snack is offered daily. Food is clean, wholesome and safe. Perishable food is held at or below 41 degrees F. Menus for regular and therapeutic diets are dated and planned at least one week ahead, posted or easily available, and resident input is encouraged. Menus as served are kept for the period the current rule requires, and at least 30 days.

definitions.definition: A modified diet ordered by the resident's healthcare provider for a medical condition, such as diabetic, low sodium, renal or texture-modified.
Food that can spoil or support bacterial growth if not kept cold or hot, such as meat, dairy, eggs, cooked vegetables and prepared salads.
The dated menu showing what was actually served, including any substitutions.

procedures: The administrator sets the meal schedule, posts it, and makes sure it gives 3 meals a day, 7 days a week. The evening meal and next morning's meal are scheduled so that no more than 14 hours pass between them (for example, an evening meal at 5:30 p.m. means breakfast is served by 7:30 a.m.). At least one nutritious snack is offered daily, and residents are told where it is available.

The food service manager or designee plans menus at least one week ahead. Each menu is dated and covers the regular diet and every therapeutic diet ordered for current residents. Menus meet the Recommended Daily Diet Allowances.

The menu is posted in a place residents can see it, or made easily available on request. The food service manager seeks resident input at least [FREQUENCY] through resident council, meal surveys or direct conversation, and records suggestions and decisions.

At admission, the nurse, administrator or designee records each resident's food preferences, allergies, chewing and swallowing problems and any ordered diet in the care plan. Therapeutic diets are provided only on the written order of the resident's healthcare provider. The order is filed in the resident record and sent to the kitchen.
The kitchen keeps an up-to-date list of residents, allergies, therapeutic diets and texture needs, and cooks check it at each meal. Diet orders are updated within [NUMBER OF] hours of a change.

Staff serving meals confirm that each resident receives the correct diet, and report to the supervisor if a resident refuses meals, is losing weight, has trouble eating or shows signs of dehydration. The supervisor notifies the resident's healthcare provider and representative as required under HLT-01.
Staff help residents who need assistance with eating, at the pace and in the position the care plan requires, and do not leave them unattended when they are at risk of choking.

Perishable food is stored at or below 41 degrees F. Staff check and record refrigerator and freezer temperatures at least daily, and discard any perishable food held above 41 degrees F beyond the safe time allowed by the Georgia food safety rules.
Food is bought from approved sources, dated when opened, stored off the floor, covered, and rotated first in, first out. Staff discard food that is spoiled, past its date or unsafe.
Kitchen staff wash hands, use clean utensils and surfaces, keep raw and cooked food separate, and follow the health and hygiene requirements in ALC-08 or PCH-07, including staying home when ill.

If a foodborne illness is suspected, the administrator saves food samples if possible, notifies the physician and the local health department as required under ALC-08 or PCH-07, and reports it to DCH if it is a serious incident (ALC-09 or PCH-08).
Each day's menu as served, including substitutions, is recorded and kept for at least 30 days, or longer if the current rule or DCH requires.
Meals are served in a dining area that is clean and comfortable. Residents who cannot or do not want to come to the dining room are offered a tray in the room and are not denied meals.
The administrator reviews food service during weekly walk-throughs and at quality-assurance meetings, including complaints, weight changes, temperature logs and menu compliance (ALC-12 or PCH-11).

responsibilities.duty: Approve the meal schedule, make sure 3 meals daily and a daily snack are served, and review food service in quality assurance.
Plan and date menus a week ahead, prepare regular and therapeutic diets, keep temperature logs and keep menus as served.
Record diet orders and allergies, serve the correct diet, assist residents and report eating or weight concerns.
Order therapeutic diets.

documentation: Posted dated weekly menus (regular and therapeutic)
Menus as served with substitutions, kept at least 30 days or longer if required
Written therapeutic diet orders in the resident record
Diet and allergy list in the kitchen
Refrigerator and freezer temperature logs
Meal schedule showing no more than 14 hours between evening and morning meals
Record of resident input on menus
Weight and eating concern notes and notifications

policies.category: Daily Living
policies.title: Activities, Social Programming and Transportation
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Communities and Personal Care Homes
policies.purpose: To make sure residents have daily social activities they choose, to protect their right to set their own schedules and take part in the wider community, and to describe how transportation, including emergency transport, is provided.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides daily social activities (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.17(4)). Residents choose which activities to join and set their own schedules, and may interact with the community outside the building (111-8-63-.25). Participation is never required. The admission agreement states the transportation provisions, and emergency transport is available at all times (111-8-63-.16). Where the community has a certified memory care center, its activity program is described in the center's program description and is designed for residents with cognitive impairment. The community keeps an activity calendar and a participation log.

definitions.definition: A planned or spontaneous event that gives residents social, recreational, creative, spiritual, physical or intellectual engagement, in a group or one-to-one.
Transportation, normally by 911 and EMS, to obtain emergency care at any time of day or night.
Scheduled rides to appointments, outings, religious services or shopping, as described in the admission agreement, including who provides them and any charge.

procedures: At admission, the administrator or activity coordinator interviews the resident and family about interests, hobbies, faith, work history, daily routine, abilities, sensory needs and cultural background, and records them in the resident's needs assessment and care plan (ADM-02). Records are updated at each reassessment.

The activity coordinator prepares a monthly activity calendar offering at least one scheduled social activity every day, including weekends and holidays, with a mix of social, physical, creative, mental and spiritual options and some activities in the evening. The calendar reflects resident requests.
The calendar is posted in common areas and in resident-accessible places, and copies are given to residents and representatives who request them. Changes are announced in advance wherever possible.

The activity coordinator seeks resident input at least [FREQUENCY] through resident council, surveys or conversation, and records suggestions and responses. Activities are changed in light of the feedback.

Residents decide whether to attend. Staff invite and encourage but do not force or penalize anyone. Residents may rest, pursue their own interests or spend time alone, and their schedules for waking, bathing, meals within the meal times and bedtime are respected as far as the care plan and staffing allow.

Staff make activities accessible, with reasonable adaptations for residents with mobility, vision, hearing, language or cognitive differences (RR-06). Residents who stay in their rooms are offered one-to-one visits, reading, music or other in-room activities.

Residents may vote, practice their faith, receive visitors and take part in community life outside the building. Staff help residents arrange these when requested, and the community does not restrict them in ways the care plan does not support.

If the community has a certified memory care center, the activity coordinator follows the program description for that center. It includes structured, familiar, low-stimulation activities matched to residents' abilities, with enough staff to supervise safely and with appropriate security for outings (HLT-02).

Outings are planned with a staff-to-resident ratio that is safe for the group and the destination. Staff bring emergency contact information, medications as ordered and a charged phone. The staffing plan is kept in line with ALC-02 or PCH-14 while the outing is in progress.

The admission agreement describes the transportation the community provides, who may drive, the charges, if any, and how to arrange a ride (RR-02). Fees for transportation are stated in advance in writing.

Emergency transportation is available at all times. Staff call 911 when a resident needs emergency care and send the face sheet, medication list and directives with the resident under HLT-01. Staff do not delay a 911 call to arrange another vehicle.

Drivers of any vehicle used for resident transport hold a valid license, have been through the background checks in STF-01, have been trained in safe loading and wheelchair securement, and are covered by the community's vehicle insurance. Vehicles are maintained, and seat belts are used for all passengers.
Staff keep a transportation log showing the date, the resident, the destination, the driver and any incident. An accident or injury in transit is handled under ALC-09 or PCH-08.

The activity coordinator records each day's activity offered and each resident's participation or reason for non-participation in the participation log. The coordinator reports to the administrator when a resident has withdrawn, declined activities or shown mood changes, and the care team considers whether the care plan needs updating.
The administrator reviews the calendar, participation log and resident feedback at each quality-assurance meeting (ALC-12 or PCH-11).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure daily activities are provided, resources are adequate, transportation terms are in the admission agreement and emergency transport is always available.
Assess interests, prepare and post the calendar, run activities, record participation and gather resident input.
Help residents attend activities they choose, respect their schedules and report withdrawal or changes in mood.
Provide safe transport, follow wheelchair securement rules and log trips.

documentation: Interest and preference information in the needs assessment and care plan
Monthly activity calendar (posted and filed)
Daily participation log with reasons for non-participation
Record of resident input and resulting changes
Admission agreement transportation provisions
Transportation log and driver qualification records
Outing staffing plans and incident reports
Memory care activity program description where applicable

policies.category: Daily Living
policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry, Furnishings and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: ALC and PCH
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident lives in a clean, safe, well-maintained building with functional furnishings and clean linens, and to meet the Georgia furnishings and safety precautions rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps the interior and exterior of the community clean, in good repair and free of unsafe conditions. Entrances, exits, sidewalks and escape routes are kept free of hazards, and the community's name and house number are visible from the street (Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. 111-8-63-.13). Furnishings are kept intact and functional. Each resident has an individual bed at least 36 x 72 inches with a mattress at least 5 inches thick (4 inches if synthetic). Cots, roll-aways, double-decks, stacked bunks, hide-a-beds and studio couches are never used in place of a bed. Each room has a closet or wardrobe, lighting adequate for reading, and a name plate outside the door unless the resident declines. Residents who need linen service receive at least 2 sheets, a pillow, pillowcase, blanket, bedspread, towels and a washcloth. Staff help residents hang pictures (111-8-63-.12). Indoor temperature is kept within the standard in the current DCH rules. This policy has no separate checklist items to tick off. It supports the physical-plant and furnishings standards that DCH reviews at unannounced inspections.

definitions.definition: Laundering and supplying bed and bath linens for a resident who cannot or does not provide their own.
Any condition that could reasonably cause injury, such as a broken step, torn flooring, exposed wiring, a blocked exit, a spill or an unsecured hazard.
Any hallway, door, ramp, stair, walkway or path residents would use to leave the building in an emergency.

procedures: The administrator or on-site manager assigns housekeeping, laundry and maintenance duties in writing on the staff schedule and reviews the assignments each month.

Before each admission, the housekeeping lead inspects the room. The room must have a bed of at least 36 x 72 inches, a mattress of at least 5 inches (4 if synthetic), a closet or wardrobe, reading-adequate lighting, and an intact, functional set of furnishings. The lead records the result on the Room Readiness Checklist.
Maintenance staff remove any cot, roll-away, double-deck, stacked bunk, hide-a-bed or studio couch from resident sleeping use. Those items are never substituted for a bed.
The housekeeping lead places a name plate outside each room at move-in. If the resident declines, the lead records the choice in the resident file.

At admission, staff identify whether the resident needs linen service. Residents who need it are issued at least 2 sheets, a pillow, pillowcase, blanket, bedspread, towels and a washcloth, and the issue is noted on the Room Readiness Checklist.
Housekeeping staff clean resident rooms and bathrooms at least weekly, and sooner when soiled. They clean common areas, kitchen, dining room and bathrooms daily. Each shift initials the cleaning log.

Linens are changed at least weekly and whenever soiled. Soiled linen is bagged at the point of use and washed separately from clean linen using the infection control practices in the health and hygiene policy (ALC-08 or PCH-07).

Staff report any damaged, unsafe or non-functional furnishing, light, lock or fixture to the on-site manager the same shift using a written maintenance request. The manager removes or repairs hazards immediately. Other repairs are completed by the date entered on the request.

The on-site manager or designee walks the interior and exterior weekly. The walk covers entrances, exits, sidewalks, ramps, parking areas and escape routes, and checks for clutter, ice, standing water, uneven surfaces, burned-out lights and debris. Findings go on the Weekly Safety Walk Log.
Hazards found on a walk are corrected or barricaded immediately. The log notes who corrected them and when.
Maintenance staff verify monthly that the community's name and house number are visible from the street, and replace or repair signage that is missing, faded or obscured.
Staff offer to help residents hang pictures and personal items. The staff member uses safe hanging methods and records any request that could not be done.

The maintenance lead checks indoor temperatures daily in resident areas and logs the readings. Out-of-range readings are reported to the administrator, who arranges repair and temporary measures such as fans, heaters or relocation.
Staff keep cleaning chemicals locked or otherwise secured away from residents, especially in memory care areas, and keep safety data sheets on site.
